title: Open-vocab rare-class AP driven by text-prior frequency, not visual grounding
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors report strong rare-class AP, but rare-class scores may be predicted by how often the class name appears in pretraining captions rather than by visual evidence quality.
hypothesis: Across LVIS rare classes, per-class AP of open-vocab detectors is better predicted by caption-corpus name frequency than by any visual difficulty measure (object size, occlusion rate); partialling out name frequency removes most of the claimed rare-class advantage.
cheapest_experiment: Take 2-3 public open-vocab detectors, compute per-class AP on LVIS val, regress against LAION/CC caption frequency of class names vs visual difficulty covariates; no training required, one GPU-day of inference.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search on existing frequency-vs-AP analyses.

title: Small-object gains from resolution are sampling-density artifacts
problem: Raising input resolution improves small-object AP, but it is unclear whether gains come from better features or simply from denser anchor/query sampling relative to object size.
hypothesis: At fixed input resolution, increasing head sampling density (smaller strides, more queries) recovers the majority of the small-object AP gain attributed to higher resolution.
cheapest_experiment: Train one detector at 640px with stride-4 head vs 1280px with stride-8 head (matched effective sampling), compare AP-small on COCO; two training runs.

title: Oracle-NMS ceiling: how much of crowded-scene error is suppression, not detection
problem: In crowded scenes it is unknown what fraction of misses are caused by duplicate suppression (NMS and its learned variants) versus the detector never firing on the instance.
hypothesis: On CrowdHuman, replacing NMS with an oracle that keeps exactly the best-matching prediction per ground-truth instance recovers a large fraction (operationally, more than a third) of missed recall, showing suppression is the dominant bottleneck.
cheapest_experiment: Run pretrained detectors on CrowdHuman, compare standard NMS output vs oracle suppression using GT matching; inference-only, under one GPU-day.

title: Synthetic occluders overestimate real occlusion robustness
problem: Occlusion robustness is often benchmarked with pasted synthetic occluders, but real occlusions have correlated geometry, shadows, and depth ordering that synthetic paste-ins lack.
hypothesis: Detector robustness measured with synthetic occluder paste-ins overestimates robustness on naturally occluded instances by a measurable margin, and the two rankings of detectors disagree.
cheapest_experiment: Build a small paired eval: naturally occluded instances (using COCO/CrowdHuman occlusion flags) vs synthetic paste-in occlusions of matched coverage fraction; evaluate 5 pretrained detectors, inference only.

title: Temporal aggregation in video detectors mostly re-ranks confidence, not fixes localization
problem: Video object detectors claim gains from temporal feature aggregation, but the mechanism of the gain (better boxes vs better scores vs recovered misses) is rarely decomposed.
hypothesis: For representative video detectors on ImageNet-VID, removing temporal aggregation at inference changes confidence ranking of already-detected boxes far more than it changes box coordinates or recovers new instances.
cheapest_experiment: Take one public video detector, log per-frame predictions with and without aggregation, decompose the AP delta into score-change, box-change, and new-detection components; inference only.

title: Open-vocab detectors fail on negated and attribute-composed prompts
problem: Open-vocabulary detection is marketed as free-form language grounding, but prompts with negation ('dog without leash') or attribute composition ('red car with open door') may be silently reduced to bag-of-words matching.
hypothesis: Open-vocab detectors score no better than a bag-of-words control (same prompt with word order shuffled and negations dropped) on a negation/composition test suite.
cheapest_experiment: Construct 200 image-prompt pairs with negations and compositions from Visual Genome attributes, evaluate 3 public open-vocab detectors against shuffled-prompt controls; annotation of 200 pairs plus inference.

title: The annotation-noise floor for tiny objects: is sub-16px AP meaningful
problem: Papers report AP improvements on tiny objects, but human annotators may disagree so much on sub-16px boxes that reported model differences sit inside the label-noise floor.
hypothesis: Inter-annotator box agreement (mean IoU) for objects under 16px falls below the 0.5 IoU matching threshold, implying AP on this stratum measures annotation style more than detection quality.
cheapest_experiment: Re-annotate 300 tiny-object instances from COCO/VisDrone with 3 annotators each, compute inter-annotator IoU distribution, compare with model-vs-GT IoU distribution; small annotation budget, no training.

title: Detection AP saturates where counting error explodes: density-conditioned evaluation
problem: Detection metrics are computed pooled over densities, hiding that per-image count error grows sharply with instance density even when AP looks flat.
hypothesis: On CrowdHuman and VisDrone, relative count error of standard detectors grows superlinearly with GT instance count while pooled AP changes little, so AP is a misleading proxy for counting-type deployments.
cheapest_experiment: Stratify existing val predictions of 5 pretrained detectors by GT count deciles, plot AP and MAE-of-count per stratum; pure re-evaluation of cached predictions.

title: Tiling for small objects: gains vs boundary double-counting
problem: Test-time tiling is the default trick for small-object detection in aerial imagery, but its accounting of objects that straddle tile boundaries is ad hoc and may inflate or deflate AP depending on the merge rule.
hypothesis: A significant share of the AP delta between tiling configurations is explained purely by boundary-object merge policy rather than by detection quality; a boundary-aware oracle merge changes tiling method rankings.
cheapest_experiment: On VisDrone/DOTA val, run one detector with 3 tile sizes and 3 merge policies, decompose AP differences into interior vs boundary strata; inference only.

title: Truncation vs occlusion: two conflated failure modes
problem: Objects cut by the image border (truncation) and objects hidden by other objects (occlusion) are usually pooled in robustness analyses although the model faces different information structure in each case.
hypothesis: Detectors show systematically different error types for truncated vs occluded instances at matched visible-area fraction: truncation mainly harms box regression while occlusion mainly harms classification confidence.
cheapest_experiment: Use datasets with truncation/occlusion flags (KITTI, CrowdHuman), match instances on visible fraction, compare localization error vs score distributions for 3 detectors; re-evaluation only.

title: Prompt-engineering variance exceeds architecture deltas in open-vocab detection
problem: Open-vocab detection papers compare architectures while quietly using different prompt templates, so the community may be ranking prompt engineering rather than methods.
hypothesis: Across a grid of reasonable prompt templates, the within-method AP spread on LVIS/ODinW is larger than the between-method spread reported in recent papers.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 public open-vocab detectors under 10 published prompt templates each on ODinW-13; inference-only grid, a few GPU-days.

title: Frame-level metrics hide flicker: temporal stability as a first-class detection metric
problem: Video detection is evaluated with per-frame mAP, which is blind to prediction flicker that dominates user-perceived and downstream-tracking quality.
hypothesis: A temporal stability metric (identity-consistent detection persistence across adjacent frames) reorders published video detectors relative to their frame-mAP ranking, i.e. frame mAP and stability are only weakly rank-correlated.
cheapest_experiment: Define stability as fraction of GT tracks with contiguous detection coverage, evaluate 5 public detectors on ImageNet-VID/OVIS val, compare rankings; inference and metric code only.

title: Small objects are detected from context, not appearance
problem: It is unknown whether detectors recognize tiny objects from their own pixels or from surrounding scene context, which changes how small-object research should be prioritized.
hypothesis: For objects under 24px, replacing the object interior with matched-statistics noise reduces detection recall by less than replacing the surrounding context ring, i.e. context carries more decision evidence than the object itself.
cheapest_experiment: Counterfactual masking study on 500 COCO/VisDrone small instances: inpaint object vs inpaint context ring, measure recall deltas for 3 pretrained detectors; inference plus cheap inpainting.

title: Amodal vs modal box conventions silently corrupt cross-dataset evaluation
problem: Datasets differ in whether boxes cover the visible region (modal) or the inferred full extent (amodal) of occluded objects, and cross-dataset evaluations ignore this label-convention shift.
hypothesis: A detector trained on modal-convention data loses AP on amodal-convention test sets primarily through localization mismatch on occluded instances, and a simple convention-translation layer recovers most of the gap.
cheapest_experiment: Cross-evaluate detectors between KITTI (amodal tendencies) and COCO-style modal data on occluded strata, then fit a per-class box scaling correction and re-measure; inference plus a linear fit.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search on convention audits.

title: Confidence calibration collapses as instance count grows
problem: Calibration of detector confidences is usually reported pooled over images; crowded images may be systematically miscalibrated, which matters for counting and safety uses.
hypothesis: Expected calibration error of matched detections grows monotonically with per-image instance count, and per-density recalibration yields better deployment thresholds than global recalibration.
cheapest_experiment: Bin existing val predictions by GT density, compute calibration curves per bin for 3 detectors on CrowdHuman; re-evaluation only.

title: Open-vocab detectors inherit bag-of-words behavior on spatial-relation prompts
problem: CLIP-like text encoders are known to behave like bag-of-words on relations; whether detection heads built on them inherit this failure for prompts like 'cup on the left of the laptop' is untested at detection granularity.
hypothesis: Open-vocab detectors localize the correct relation argument no better than chance between the two candidate objects when the prompt specifies a spatial relation.
cheapest_experiment: Build 300 two-object relation prompts from Visual Genome relations, test whether the top box matches the relation-specified instance vs the distractor; inference only.

title: Extreme aspect ratios: wires, poles, and the IoU-anchor blind spot
problem: Very elongated objects (cables, rails, poles) are poorly served both by IoU matching (thin structures get near-zero IoU under small offsets) and by anchor/query priors, yet they matter for inspection and AV domains.
hypothesis: For objects with aspect ratio above 10:1, match rate under IoU 0.5 is dominated by annotation and matching geometry rather than by detector quality: perturbing GT boxes by one pixel width changes AP more than swapping detectors.
cheapest_experiment: On a wire/pole subset (from TTPLA or similar public data), measure AP sensitivity to 1-2px GT perturbations vs detector swaps; re-evaluation only.

title: Motion-blur-stratified evaluation for video detection
problem: Video detectors are trained and evaluated on frames sampled without regard to motion blur, so reported AP hides a blur-conditional failure mode central to real video.
hypothesis: AP conditioned on estimated per-frame blur magnitude declines steeply for image-pretrained detectors, and this decline, not average AP, predicts which detectors win on high-motion deployment footage.
cheapest_experiment: Estimate blur (variance-of-Laplacian or optical-flow magnitude) on ImageNet-VID val frames, stratify AP for 4 detectors; re-evaluation only.

title: Copy-paste augmentation gains: appearance learning or label rebalancing
problem: Copy-paste augmentation improves detection and segmentation, but the mechanism (more minority-class instances vs new appearance contexts) is unresolved, which determines whether cheaper resampling suffices.
hypothesis: Class-frequency-matched resampling of whole images recovers the majority of copy-paste AP gains, showing rebalancing, not novel composition, is the active ingredient.
cheapest_experiment: Three matched training runs on COCO (baseline, copy-paste, frequency-matched resampling) with one mid-size detector; three training runs on a modest budget.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search on existing copy-paste ablations.

title: Zero-shot claims and caption leakage: measuring test-class exposure in pretraining
problem: Open-vocab detectors claim zero-shot generalization to held-out classes, but pretraining caption corpora likely contain those class names with images, making 'zero-shot' an exposure-frequency statement rather than a capability claim.
hypothesis: Per-class zero-shot AP correlates strongly with the count of pretraining captions containing the class name, and truly unexposed synthetic class names (novel coinages bound to visual concepts) show near-zero transfer.
cheapest_experiment: For one open detector with public pretraining data, count caption matches per held-out class and correlate with AP; then test 20 invented-name classes via prompt-tuned references; mostly counting plus inference.

title: Synonym collisions in open-vocab NMS: person vs pedestrian
problem: Open-vocab detectors run class-wise NMS over user-supplied vocabularies; synonymous or overlapping class names (person, pedestrian, human) create duplicate boxes that closed-set evaluation never sees.
hypothesis: Adding synonyms of existing classes to the inference vocabulary measurably degrades effective precision because duplicates survive class-wise suppression, and class-agnostic NMS over text-embedding clusters repairs most of the damage.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 2 open-vocab detectors on COCO with vocabulary augmented by 2 synonyms per class, measure duplicate rate and AP under class-wise vs embedding-clustered NMS; inference only.

title: Visible-fraction confounds in reported occlusion robustness
problem: Occlusion robustness comparisons rarely control for visible-area fraction, so a method may look occlusion-robust simply because its evaluation instances are less occluded.
hypothesis: After matching instances on visible fraction, published occlusion-robustness gaps between representative methods shrink substantially, and some method orderings reverse.
cheapest_experiment: Use amodal datasets (KINS, COCOA) to bin instances by visible fraction and re-evaluate 4 detectors within bins; re-evaluation only.

title: The impossibility zone: objects smaller than effective stride
problem: There should exist an object-size regime where detection is information-theoretically crippled by feature stride and antialiasing, but this zone has not been mapped empirically as a function of architecture.
hypothesis: Recall falls to near-zero when object size drops below a constant multiple of the finest feature stride, and this breakpoint is predicted by architecture geometry rather than training data volume.
cheapest_experiment: Synthetic controlled dataset with objects of parametric size on real backgrounds; evaluate detectors with strides 4/8/16 without retraining where possible and with short finetunes otherwise; small compute.

title: Density distribution shift between train and test in crowded benchmarks
problem: Crowded-scene benchmarks may have different density distributions in train vs test, so models implicitly tuned to train-set density profiles get flattering scores that do not reflect density generalization.
hypothesis: Reweighting the CrowdHuman test set to alternative density profiles (uniform over density deciles) changes the ranking of published detectors.
cheapest_experiment: Compute density histograms of train/test, re-weight per-image AP contributions of 5 detectors under uniform-density weighting; pure re-analysis.

title: Error decomposition for video detection mAP: association vs detection
problem: Video detection scores mix per-frame detection failures with temporal inconsistency, and no standard decomposition tool attributes the loss between them.
hypothesis: For modern video detectors, the majority of the gap to oracle performance comes from temporally inconsistent confidence (same object, fluctuating score) rather than from frames where the object is entirely missed.
cheapest_experiment: Implement an oracle that stabilizes scores along GT tracks (max-pooled confidence) and measure the mAP recovered vs an oracle that fills fully-missed frames; inference-only analysis on ImageNet-VID.

title: Detectors cannot say 'nothing here': rejection of undetectable prompts
problem: Open-vocab detectors are always evaluated on prompts that exist in the image; their behavior when the queried class is absent (the everyday deployment case) is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Given prompts for absent classes, open-vocab detectors produce above-threshold false detections at rates that make them unusable for verification-style tasks, and the false-fire rate is uncorrelated with their standard AP.
cheapest_experiment: Query 3 detectors with 50 absent-class prompts per image over 1,000 COCO images, measure false-fire rate vs prompt semantic distance to image content; inference only.

title: Aerial vs natural small objects: one scaling law does not fit both
problem: Small-object methods validated on COCO-small are assumed to transfer to aerial imagery, but the two regimes differ in context density, object orientation statistics, and background clutter.
hypothesis: Method rankings on COCO-small and on VisDrone/DOTA small strata are only weakly rank-correlated, refuting the assumption that COCO-small is a proxy for aerial small-object detection.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 6 public detectors on both small-object strata and compute rank correlation; inference only.

title: Occlusion ordering as an unsupervised probe of detector 3D awareness
problem: Whether 2D detectors encode depth ordering of overlapping instances is unknown, yet it constrains what monocular pipelines can extract for free.
hypothesis: A linear probe on frozen detector instance features predicts pairwise occlusion order significantly above chance, and probe accuracy correlates with the detector's crowded-scene AP.
cheapest_experiment: Extract instance features for overlapping pairs on COCOA/KINS with known order, train a linear probe, correlate with crowded AP across 5 detectors; feature extraction plus logistic regression.

title: Object permanence in long video: detectors plus trackers vs a Kalman baseline
problem: Modern detect-then-track stacks are assumed to handle temporary occlusion, but their object-permanence behavior over multi-second occlusions is rarely quantified against classical prediction.
hypothesis: For occlusion gaps above 2 seconds, a constant-velocity Kalman coaster on last-seen boxes rehits reappearing objects at higher rates than the learned re-association of common tracker stacks.
cheapest_experiment: On MOT17/DanceTrack val, extract occlusion gap events, compare re-acquisition rates of stock trackers vs a 50-line Kalman coaster; analysis only.

title: Fixed query budgets impose an instance-count ceiling on DETR-family models
problem: Query-based detectors allocate a fixed number of object queries; their degradation profile as scene instance count approaches and exceeds the query budget is not systematically characterized.
hypothesis: Recall of DETR-family detectors degrades sharply and superlinearly once GT count exceeds roughly half the query budget, at densities where dense-prediction detectors degrade gracefully.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 query-based and 2 dense detectors on CrowdHuman stratified by GT count, and re-run one query model with 2x and 4x queries at inference; mostly inference.

title: Do feature-upsampling modules improve localization or classification for small objects
problem: Papers proposing feature upsampling or fusion for small objects report AP but never separate whether the gain lands in localization or classification, leaving the mechanism unclear.
hypothesis: Most AP-small gains from upsampling modules come from higher recall at fixed localization quality (classification/objectness), not from tighter boxes; localization error conditioned on detection is unchanged.
cheapest_experiment: Use TIDE-style error decomposition on published checkpoints with and without such modules on COCO; re-evaluation only.

title: AP-rare on LVIS is statistically unstable at current test sizes
problem: LVIS rare classes contribute a handful of test instances each, so headline AP-rare differences between methods may be inside sampling noise, yet drive publication claims.
hypothesis: Bootstrap confidence intervals on AP-rare for representative methods overlap for most published pairwise comparisons, i.e. the community is ranking noise.
cheapest_experiment: Bootstrap-resample LVIS val images 1,000 times, compute AP-rare CIs for 6 public checkpoints; pure re-analysis of cached predictions.

title: Does amodal completion pretraining causally improve occluded detection
problem: It is often asserted that reasoning about hidden object parts should help occluded-object detection, but no controlled causal test exists at matched compute.
hypothesis: Pretraining a detector backbone with an amodal mask-completion objective improves occluded-strata AP over a modal-mask control at matched compute, and the gain is specific to occluded instances.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched pretrainings (amodal vs modal completion on COCOA/KINS) followed by identical detection finetunes; two modest training runs.

title: Temporal modeling gains vanish under strong single-frame backbones
problem: Video detection architectures were validated with weak backbones; whether temporal modules still add value on top of modern strong single-frame features is an open, deployment-relevant question.
hypothesis: At matched inference compute, a strong single-frame detector matches or beats the same detector plus temporal aggregation modules on standard video detection benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Train or reuse a modern backbone detector, compare frame-only vs one representative temporal aggregation head at matched FLOPs on ImageNet-VID; one or two finetune runs.

title: Compression-stratified detection curves as a standard report
problem: Deployed detection consumes compressed streams, but benchmarks evaluate on high-quality JPEGs, hiding that small objects degrade first under compression.
hypothesis: AP-small decays with bitrate at a rate several times steeper than AP-large, and the crossover bitrate where model rankings change lies inside the range used by common CCTV systems.
cheapest_experiment: Re-encode COCO val at 6 bitrates (H.264 or JPEG quality ladder), evaluate 5 pretrained detectors, plot size-stratified AP-vs-bitrate; inference only.

title: Ignore regions teach detectors miscalibrated confidence
problem: Crowded datasets use ignore regions for unannotatable areas; training samples overlapping these regions receive no gradient, which may systematically distort learned confidence in dense areas.
hypothesis: Detectors trained with ignore regions are overconfident inside dense regions relative to sparse regions at matched visual difficulty, and replacing ignore with soft labels reduces the gap.
cheapest_experiment: Compare calibration inside vs outside former ignore-region-like density strata on CrowdHuman for existing checkpoints, then one retraining run with soft-label treatment; one training run.

title: Hierarchical label confusion is mis-scored in open-vocab evaluation
problem: When a model answers 'animal' for a 'dog' box, current matching counts a full classification error, though the answer is partially correct in the label hierarchy; open-vocab settings make this ubiquitous.
hypothesis: Scoring with hierarchy-aware credit (WordNet path similarity) changes the ranking of open-vocab detectors, because methods differ mainly in label granularity behavior rather than grounding quality.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score existing predictions of 4 open-vocab detectors on LVIS with hierarchy-aware matching; re-analysis only.

title: Axis-aligned IoU systematically undervalues oriented detection of elongated objects
problem: Communities using axis-aligned boxes evaluate elongated rotated objects (ships, vehicles from above) with a geometry that punishes correct oriented detections, distorting progress measures.
hypothesis: For objects with aspect ratio above 4:1 and orientation far from axis-aligned, the achievable axis-aligned IoU of a perfect oriented detection is bounded well below common thresholds, and dataset score gaps between oriented and axis-aligned methods are mostly geometric artifacts.
cheapest_experiment: Analytic computation of IoU bounds as a function of aspect ratio and angle, plus re-scoring DOTA predictions under both geometries; analysis only.

title: Saliency-biased backbones and the camouflage blind spot
problem: Pretrained backbones are optimized on photographer-curated, salient-object imagery, which may impose a saliency prior that structurally limits camouflaged and low-contrast object detection.
hypothesis: Detection recall on camouflaged objects correlates negatively with a backbone saliency-bias score (how strongly its features separate salient from non-salient regions), across backbones at matched detection AP on COCO.
cheapest_experiment: Compute a saliency-bias probe on 6 frozen backbones, finetune identical detection heads briefly, evaluate on COD10K; probes plus short finetunes.

title: Episodic variance makes most few-shot detection deltas unreadable
problem: Few-shot detection results depend heavily on which support examples are sampled, and papers report single-episode or few-episode results, so many claimed improvements may be sampling luck.
hypothesis: The across-episode standard deviation of few-shot detection AP exceeds the median published method-to-method improvement on standard benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Re-run 3 public few-shot detection methods over 30 support-set episodes each on standard splits, report variance vs published deltas; moderate inference plus light finetuning per episode.

title: AP integrates over operating points nobody deploys
problem: AP averages precision over all recall levels, including confidence regimes never used in deployment, so leaderboard AP can diverge from utility at any deployable threshold.
hypothesis: Rankings of published detectors by AP and by F1-at-best-fixed-threshold disagree for a substantial fraction of model pairs, and the disagreement grows on long-tail data.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score cached predictions of 10 public detectors on COCO and LVIS under fixed-threshold F1 and compare rank orders with AP; pure re-analysis.

title: Deriving the IoU threshold from annotation noise instead of tradition
problem: The 0.5 IoU threshold is a historical convention; a principled threshold should depend on the annotation noise level of each dataset, which varies by domain and object size.
hypothesis: Setting the matching threshold at the dataset-specific inter-annotator IoU quantile changes which methods rank highest on at least one major benchmark, showing conclusions are threshold-convention artifacts.
cheapest_experiment: Estimate inter-annotator IoU from existing double-annotated subsets (or re-annotate 500 boxes), re-score public predictions at the derived thresholds; small annotation plus re-analysis.

title: Dice on small structures is a coin flip: size-stratified segmentation reporting
problem: Dice on tiny structures is dominated by a few boundary pixels, so aggregate Dice hides that small-structure segmentation may be statistically meaningless at current annotation quality.
hypothesis: For structures under 100 pixels, the across-annotator Dice between human experts is as low as the model-vs-annotator Dice, implying no measurable model deficit in that stratum.
cheapest_experiment: Use existing multi-annotator medical sets (LIDC) to compute size-stratified human-human vs model-human Dice; re-analysis of public data.

title: The 101-point AP interpolation bias in low-data regimes
problem: COCO AP uses 101-point interpolated precision, which introduces a small but systematic bias whose magnitude relative to reported deltas in few-shot and rare-class settings is unknown.
hypothesis: In evaluations with under 100 positive instances per class, interpolation choice (101-point vs exact area) shifts AP by amounts comparable to published method improvements.
cheapest_experiment: Recompute AP under both integration rules for rare LVIS classes and few-shot benchmarks with cached predictions; re-analysis only.

title: Macro-mAP vs instance-weighted detection quality: whose average is it
problem: mAP averages per-class AP equally regardless of class frequency, silently encoding a value judgment; nobody has measured how much leaderboard order depends on that judgment.
hypothesis: Switching between macro (per-class) and micro (instance-weighted) averaging reorders published COCO/LVIS leaderboards, and papers claiming long-tail progress benefit disproportionately from the macro convention.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score 15 public checkpoints under both averaging schemes; re-analysis only.

title: Annotation-noise-propagated confidence intervals for COCO AP
problem: Benchmarks report AP as a point estimate with no uncertainty from annotation noise, so the community cannot tell which SOTA increments are inside the label-noise band.
hypothesis: Propagating measured annotation noise (from multi-annotator re-labeling of a COCO subset) into AP yields uncertainty bands of roughly comparable magnitude to typical year-over-year SOTA increments, rendering many claims indistinguishable.
cheapest_experiment: Triple-annotate 1,000 COCO val images, estimate a box/label noise model, Monte-Carlo perturb the GT and recompute AP bands for 10 checkpoints; modest annotation budget plus re-analysis.

title: When does boundary quality matter: an adoption analysis for Boundary IoU
problem: Boundary IoU exists but the field defaults to mask IoU; there is no systematic map of the task regimes where the two metrics rank methods differently, so adoption arguments are anecdotal.
hypothesis: Mask IoU and Boundary IoU rankings diverge primarily for large objects and articulated categories, and metric choice flips the winner in a nontrivial fraction of published segmentation comparisons.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score public instance segmentation predictions under both metrics stratified by size and category; re-analysis only.

title: Detector confidences are not comparable across models, breaking threshold-based comparisons
problem: Comparisons at a shared confidence threshold implicitly assume comparable score scales across detectors, but score distributions differ wildly by loss and architecture, contaminating deployment-style evaluations.
hypothesis: After per-model calibration to a common reference (matched precision on a calibration split), threshold-based comparisons of detectors change conclusions relative to naive shared-threshold comparisons in a majority of cases.
cheapest_experiment: Take 8 public detectors, compare naive threshold-0.5 F1 vs calibrated-threshold F1 rankings on COCO val; re-analysis only.

title: AP rewards hedging: low-confidence box spam as metric gaming
problem: Because AP only requires correct ranking, emitting large numbers of low-confidence boxes can raise AP while making deployment strictly worse; the size of this wedge is unquantified.
hypothesis: Appending calibrated low-confidence guesses to a detector output raises COCO AP measurably while lowering fixed-threshold F1 and increasing deployment review cost, demonstrating AP is gameable by hedging.
cheapest_experiment: Post-process one detector output by adding region-proposal boxes with epsilon confidence, measure AP and F1 deltas; re-analysis only.

title: Crowd and ignore-region handling differs across eval implementations
problem: COCO-style crowd flags and ignore regions are handled differently across evaluation codebases, potentially producing silent AP differences attributed to models.
hypothesis: The same prediction file scored by different popular evaluation implementations differs by up to a few tenths of AP, exceeding some published improvements.
cheapest_experiment: Score identical prediction files with pycocotools, a common reimplementation, and one framework-internal evaluator; diff the outputs per class; pure software study.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search on existing evaluator audits.

title: Dice vs boundary-F1 disagreement as a taxonomy of segmentation errors
problem: Dice and boundary-F1 are used interchangeably, but they respond to different error types; the field lacks a quantitative map of when they disagree and which error types drive it.
hypothesis: Method rankings under Dice and boundary-F1 disagree systematically for categories with thin protrusions and holes, and the disagreement can be predicted from a shape-complexity statistic of the class.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score public segmentation predictions under both metrics per class, regress ranking disagreement on shape complexity; re-analysis only.

title: Panoptic Quality is unstable for rare things: decomposing PQ noise
problem: PQ multiplies recognition and segmentation terms, amplifying noise for classes with few instances, but the variance structure of PQ has not been characterized against method deltas.
hypothesis: Bootstrap variance of per-class PQ for rare classes exceeds the typical between-method PQ differences reported on standard panoptic benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Bootstrap image resampling over cached panoptic predictions of 5 methods; re-analysis only.

title: AP is not a proper scoring rule for detection: constructing and measuring exploitation
problem: A metric is trustworthy if truthful reporting of beliefs maximizes it; AP with greedy matching may be exploitable by strategic score shaping, but no one has quantified real-model exploitation headroom.
hypothesis: There exists a post-hoc, information-free transformation of a detector's scores and box set that raises AP on standard benchmarks, proving AP violates propriety in practice, and its magnitude is comparable to typical SOTA gaps.
cheapest_experiment: Optimize a score-reshaping and duplicate-injection wrapper on val predictions of one detector, measure AP gain and confirm no new information is used; re-analysis only.

title: Disentangled evaluation: separate leaderboards for finding, naming, and outlining
problem: Detection metrics conflate whether models find objects, name them correctly, and outline them tightly; a method can win by trading one for another invisibly.
hypothesis: Under a disentangled protocol (class-agnostic recall, naming accuracy given location, localization tightness given match), current SOTA rankings differ per axis, and no single model dominates all three.
cheapest_experiment: Implement the three-axis scoring on cached predictions of 10 public models; re-analysis only.

title: A fresh i.i.d. test set for COCO: measuring a decade of adaptive overfitting
problem: COCO has served as a fixed target for ten years; the community-wide degree of adaptive overfitting to its idiosyncrasies is unknown for detection (analogous studies exist for classification).
hypothesis: On a newly collected test set matched to the COCO distribution and annotation protocol, absolute AP drops for all models, and the drop is larger for models developed later, indicating cumulative benchmark adaptation.
cheapest_experiment: Collect and annotate 2,000 new images under the original COCO protocol, evaluate a historical sequence of 15 public checkpoints; annotation cost dominated, no training.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search for existing COCO replication studies.

title: Arbitrary size buckets: continuous size-AP curves change conclusions
problem: AP-small/medium/large use fixed area cutoffs (32^2, 96^2) chosen historically; conclusions about which methods help small objects may not survive a continuous treatment of size.
hypothesis: Methods claimed to improve small-object AP show gains concentrated in a narrow band near the bucket boundary, and continuous size-AP curves reveal crossovers hidden by the bucketed report.
cheapest_experiment: Compute AP in sliding size windows from cached predictions of small-object-oriented methods vs baselines; re-analysis only.

title: Missing annotations punish better detectors: the unlabeled-object tax
problem: Benchmarks contain unlabeled true objects; detectors good enough to find them are charged with false positives, meaning the metric may actively penalize detection improvements beyond the annotation frontier.
hypothesis: Human verification of high-confidence 'false positives' shows that stronger detectors have a higher fraction of correct-but-unlabeled detections, so measured precision gaps understate true gaps and can invert rankings near the frontier.
cheapest_experiment: Sample 500 top-scoring false positives from each of 5 detectors on COCO val, human-verify them, recompute corrected precision; small annotation budget.

title: Duplicate-annotation policies are a hidden metric hyperparameter
problem: Datasets contain near-duplicate GT boxes handled by ad hoc dedup policies during evaluation; the sensitivity of scores to this policy is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Varying the GT dedup policy (IoU threshold for merging duplicate annotations) within reasonable bounds changes per-class AP by more than published deltas for affected classes.
cheapest_experiment: Detect near-duplicate GT pairs in COCO/LVIS, re-score cached predictions under 3 dedup policies; re-analysis only.

title: Slice-wise vs volume-wise aggregation flips 3D medical segmentation rankings
problem: 3D medical segmentation results are aggregated per-slice, per-volume, or per-dataset with little standardization, and the aggregation axis interacts with lesion-size distributions.
hypothesis: For public 3D benchmarks, per-slice and per-volume Dice aggregation produce different method rankings whenever lesion size distributions are heavy-tailed, and the flip direction is predictable from that distribution.
cheapest_experiment: Re-aggregate cached predictions from public medical segmentation challenges under both schemes; re-analysis only.

title: ECE for detection is ill-posed: ground calibration in downstream decision cost
problem: Expected calibration error for detectors requires choosing which predictions count and how they match GT, and different choices give contradictory conclusions; calibration should instead be measured by decision cost in a task.
hypothesis: Across plausible ECE variants for detection, method rankings disagree, while a decision-theoretic evaluation (expected cost over a threshold-decision task with specified error costs) yields a stable ranking that ECE variants fail to predict.
cheapest_experiment: Implement 4 ECE variants and one expected-cost metric over cached predictions of 8 detectors; re-analysis only.

title: mAP is blind to score magnitudes: what monotone-invariance hides
problem: mAP is invariant to monotone transforms of confidence, so two detectors with identical mAP can differ enormously in usable-confidence quality, which downstream systems depend on.
hypothesis: Among public detector pairs with near-identical mAP, downstream utility (selective-prediction risk-coverage area) differs substantially, demonstrating that mAP-equal is not deployment-equal.
cheapest_experiment: Find mAP-matched detector pairs among public checkpoints, compare risk-coverage curves on COCO val; re-analysis only.

title: Does average recall of proposals still predict final AP for modern detectors
problem: The proposal-quality metric AR was validated as a proxy for final detection AP in the two-stage era; whether that correlation survives modern end-to-end and query-based pipelines is untested.
hypothesis: Across modern architectures, AR of intermediate proposals correlates only weakly with final AP, breaking a folk rule still used to justify proposal-stage research.
cheapest_experiment: Extract proposal-stage AR and final AP for 8 public models spanning architectures, compute correlation; inference only.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search for the original AR-AP correlation claims.

title: Cost-sensitive AP: confusion costs from real applications
problem: AP charges all class confusions equally, but confusing a person with a pole is not the same as confusing two furniture types in safety domains; there is no standard cost-weighted detection metric grounded in application data.
hypothesis: Under application-derived confusion cost matrices (from AV incident taxonomies), model rankings differ from mAP rankings, and some widely-used models are dominated once costs are considered.
cheapest_experiment: Build one cost matrix from public AV safety taxonomies, re-score cached nuScenes/COCO-person predictions; re-analysis only.

title: Image-level vs instance-level bootstrap: which CI is right for detection
problem: Confidence intervals for detection metrics can resample images or instances, and the two choices give different intervals because instances within an image are correlated; the field has no standard.
hypothesis: Instance-level bootstrap systematically underestimates the variance of AP relative to image-level bootstrap by a factor large enough to change significance conclusions in typical comparisons.
cheapest_experiment: Run both bootstrap schemes on cached predictions over COCO val for 5 models, compare interval widths and pairwise significance verdicts; re-analysis only.

title: A survey and re-analysis of significance testing in detection papers
problem: It is unknown what fraction of detection papers report any statistical uncertainty, and what fraction of their headline claims survive proper tests; this is measurable meta-science, not opinion.
hypothesis: Fewer than one in ten recent detection papers report variance or tests, and among reproducible claims, a nontrivial fraction fail an image-level bootstrap test at conventional levels.
cheapest_experiment: Systematically code 200 recent detection papers for statistical practice, re-test 20 claims with public checkpoints; reading time plus re-analysis.

title: Most SOTA claims are Pareto-incomparable: multi-metric honesty
problem: Single-number metrics manufacture total orders over methods that are actually incomparable across relevant axes (AP, calibration, latency, small-object AP, robustness).
hypothesis: Under a 5-axis evaluation, the majority of consecutive SOTA claims on COCO in recent years are Pareto-incomparable with their predecessor, i.e. they trade one axis for another rather than dominating.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate a historical chain of 12 public checkpoints on 5 axes with cached inference; re-analysis plus corruption evaluation.

title: Tracking metrics are threshold-tuned on test: MOTA/HOTA sensitivity audit
problem: Multi-object tracking metrics depend on detection score thresholds that many submissions tune against the evaluation itself, making leaderboard gaps partially an artifact of threshold search.
hypothesis: Re-evaluating public trackers with thresholds tuned only on a held-out split shrinks leaderboard gaps substantially and reorders mid-table methods.
cheapest_experiment: Take 8 public tracker outputs, re-tune thresholds on a val split, score on test split; re-analysis only.

title: Synonym mismatches counted as errors in open-vocab evaluation
problem: Open-vocab evaluation string-matches predicted labels to GT vocabulary, counting synonyms and lexical variants as failures, which penalizes exactly the models with richer vocabularies.
hypothesis: Fuzzy label matching (embedding or WordNet synonym sets) raises measured AP of generative-vocabulary detectors substantially more than fixed-vocabulary ones, changing cross-paradigm comparisons.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score cached open-vocab predictions with synonym-aware matching on LVIS/ODinW; re-analysis only.

title: Box AP overstates localization quality for articulated objects
problem: A tight box on an articulated object (spread limbs, tails) can contain mostly background, so box IoU signals localization quality that masks would contradict; the size of this distortion is unquantified.
hypothesis: For high-articulation categories, box-IoU-matched detections show mask-IoU distributions substantially lower than for compact categories, and box AP overstates cross-category localization progress accordingly.
cheapest_experiment: Use COCO instances with both boxes and masks, compare box-IoU vs mask-IoU joint distributions per category from cached predictions; re-analysis only.

title: Minimum detectable effect: power analysis tables for popular benchmarks
problem: Reviewers and authors have no reference for the smallest AP difference a benchmark can statistically resolve, so undersized test sets keep supporting unresolvable claims.
hypothesis: For several popular domain benchmarks, the minimum detectable AP difference at conventional power exceeds 1 point, larger than many published improvements evaluated on them.
cheapest_experiment: Estimate metric variance by bootstrap on public predictions per benchmark, derive minimum detectable effects, publish lookup tables; re-analysis only.

title: Is SOTA above the human agreement ceiling, and what does that mean
problem: If model-vs-GT agreement exceeds human-vs-human agreement on a benchmark, further gains measure fit to annotation idiosyncrasies rather than perception; benchmarks lack this ceiling measurement.
hypothesis: On at least one major detection benchmark, current SOTA model-GT agreement exceeds measured human-human agreement, implying the benchmark has become a label-style-matching contest.
cheapest_experiment: Re-annotate 500 images with independent annotators, compute human-human AP against original GT, compare with SOTA model AP; small annotation budget.

title: NMS and threshold tuning as unreported test leakage
problem: Post-processing hyperparameters (NMS IoU, score floors, top-k) are commonly tuned per benchmark, effectively fitting the test distribution while the paper narrative credits the architecture.
hypothesis: Standardizing post-processing across methods (single shared configuration tuned on a neutral split) shrinks published between-method gaps on COCO by a measurable fraction and reorders some pairs.
cheapest_experiment: Re-run post-processing sweeps for 8 public checkpoints under a shared protocol; re-analysis only.

title: The empty-mask convention silently decides medical segmentation winners
problem: When GT and prediction are both empty, Dice is defined by convention (1, 0, or excluded), and conventions differ across papers; in screening datasets with many negatives this choice can dominate scores.
hypothesis: On public medical benchmarks with high negative-slice fractions, switching empty-case conventions changes method rankings, and some published cross-paper comparisons are invalid because they mix conventions.
cheapest_experiment: Re-aggregate cached predictions from 2 public challenges under the 3 conventions; re-analysis only, plus a survey of which papers use which.

title: AP at IoU 0.5:0.95 weights localization unevenly across object sizes
problem: Averaging AP over IoU 0.5 to 0.95 is treated as balanced, but a fixed IoU increment corresponds to very different pixel tolerances at different object sizes, embedding a hidden size weighting.
hypothesis: Under a pixel-tolerance-equalized IoU ladder (thresholds scheduled by object size), method rankings differ from the standard ladder, revealing that some 'localization improvements' are large-object-specific artifacts.
cheapest_experiment: Define the equalized ladder analytically, re-score cached predictions of 8 detectors; re-analysis only.

title: Evaluation-server vs local-eval discrepancies as a reproducibility hazard
problem: Test-server evaluations occasionally disagree with local val-based expectations for reasons beyond distribution shift (version drift, flag handling), but no audit quantifies this channel.
hypothesis: For benchmarks offering both, the server-vs-local metric discrepancy on identical prediction files is nonzero for a measurable fraction of submissions and correlates with use of nonstandard prediction formats.
cheapest_experiment: Submit identical files to servers and score locally across 3 benchmarks and several format variants; submission quota plus re-analysis.

title: Annotation style drift across dataset versions invalidates cross-version claims
problem: Datasets evolve across releases (COCO 2014 vs 2017 splits, LVIS versions), and annotation-style drift between versions may masquerade as method progress in papers comparing across versions.
hypothesis: The same model evaluated on matched images labeled under two dataset versions scores differently by an amount comparable to typical claimed improvements, driven by identifiable annotation-style changes.
cheapest_experiment: Find images present in both versions, evaluate 5 checkpoints against each version's labels; re-analysis only.

title: Minimum-support reporting standards for tail metrics
problem: AP over classes with under 10 test instances is routinely reported to two decimals without support disclosure; a standard is needed and its adoption case should be empirical, not rhetorical.
hypothesis: Enforcing a minimum-support rule (report AP only for classes above a support threshold, otherwise pooled) changes the qualitative conclusions of a meaningful fraction of recent long-tail papers.
cheapest_experiment: Re-aggregate published per-class results under the rule using cached predictions; re-analysis only.

title: Does benchmark AP predict downstream utility: grasping and safety as ground truth
problem: The community assumes benchmark AP transfers to downstream utility, but direct measurements linking AP to task success (robotic grasping, AV intervention rates) are scarce and old.
hypothesis: Across detectors spanning 10 AP points, downstream task success in a fixed pipeline saturates or becomes noise-dominated well before the top of the AP range, meaning marginal AP no longer buys utility.
cheapest_experiment: Fix a simulated grasping or driving pipeline, swap 6 public detectors, measure task metrics; simulation compute only.

title: Why probabilistic detection metrics failed to be adopted: an empirical autopsy
problem: Metrics like PDQ that reward spatial and semantic uncertainty were proposed and largely ignored; understanding whether the barrier is conceptual, practical, or evidential would inform future metric design.
hypothesis: On modern detectors, PDQ-style metrics identify uncertainty-quality differences invisible to mAP, and their non-adoption is attributable to tooling friction rather than lack of signal, measurable by correlating PDQ deltas with downstream selective-prediction utility.
cheapest_experiment: Score 8 public detectors with a PDQ implementation, correlate with risk-coverage utility, and survey tooling friction; re-analysis only.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search on PDQ follow-up literature.

title: GT tightness conventions vary within single datasets: an intra-dataset audit
problem: Within one dataset, annotators differ in how tightly boxes hug objects and whether hidden parts are included, creating per-annotator label styles that models can partially learn and metrics cannot see.
hypothesis: Annotator-identity (or batch) signatures are recoverable from GT box statistics, and model AP differs measurably across annotator strata, proving that part of AP measures style matching.
cheapest_experiment: Cluster GT boxes by style features (relative margin, aspect handling), evaluate models per cluster on COCO val; re-analysis only.

title: Does better classification pretraining actually help dense tasks: a rank-correlation audit
problem: The community assumes backbones with higher ImageNet or zero-shot classification accuracy transfer better to detection and segmentation, but systematic compute-matched evidence across modern backbone families is thin.
hypothesis: Across 15 backbones at matched detection-finetune compute, the rank correlation between upstream classification accuracy and COCO AP is weak (below 0.5), and breaks down entirely within a backbone family at fixed scale.
cheapest_experiment: Finetune identical detection heads on 15 public backbones with a fixed short schedule, correlate upstream vs downstream metrics; roughly 15 short training runs.

title: Mapping where SAM zero-shot actually works: a falsification atlas
problem: The claim that SAM generalizes zero-shot to arbitrary domains is repeated without a systematic domain map; practitioners need to know the boundary of validity, not anecdotes.
hypothesis: SAM-family zero-shot mask quality degrades below usability (mask IoU under 0.5 against expert labels) on a predictable subset of domains characterized by low edge contrast and non-photographic sensors (ultrasound, sonar, electron microscopy), and prompt engineering does not rescue it.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate SAM variants on 12 public domain datasets with existing GT, plot quality vs domain descriptors; inference only.

title: Is more finetuning data always better: the noisy-web-data inflection point
problem: Detection practitioners assume more training data monotonically helps, but web-mined detection data carries label noise whose marginal harm may eventually exceed marginal signal.
hypothesis: AP as a function of added web-mined training data is non-monotonic: past an inflection point that depends on noise rate, additional data lowers AP on a clean test set.
cheapest_experiment: Mix COCO with increasing fractions of auto-labeled web images at measured noise rates, train fixed short schedules, trace the curve; 5-6 short training runs.

title: Does mask supervision causally improve box detection
problem: It is folklore that adding instance-mask supervision improves box AP, but modern evidence at matched annotation budget (masks cost more than boxes) is missing.
hypothesis: At matched annotation cost (fewer masked images vs more boxed images), box-only training beats box-plus-mask training on box AP, reversing the folklore once cost is accounted.
cheapest_experiment: Three matched-budget training runs on COCO subsets (boxes only, masks on all, cost-matched mix); three modest training runs.

title: Is multi-scale training still necessary with modern backbones
problem: Multi-scale training is inherited as mandatory for detection, but strong pretrained backbones with heavy augmentation may have made it redundant, and it complicates pipelines and batching.
hypothesis: With a modern pretrained backbone and standard augmentation, single-scale training matches multi-scale training on COCO AP within noise at matched compute.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs (single-scale vs multi-scale) at two backbone scales; four training runs total.

title: Frozen foundation backbones for detection: is finetuning overrated
problem: The assumption that detection requires backbone finetuning predates strong self-supervised foundations; freezing would enable massive multi-task reuse if the penalty is small.
hypothesis: A frozen modern foundation backbone with a trained adapter and detection head reaches within 2 AP of full finetuning on COCO at matched total compute, and beats it under domain shift.
cheapest_experiment: Two training runs (frozen-plus-adapter vs full finetune) with one strong backbone, evaluated in-domain and on corruption/shift suites; two training runs.

title: Longer detection training past the recipe: mapping the overfitting onset
problem: Recipes assume detection benefits from long schedules, but the shape of the AP-vs-epochs curve past standard schedules on COCO-scale data with modern augmentation is unmeasured public knowledge.
hypothesis: For COCO-scale data, validation AP plateaus and then declines measurably within 3x standard schedule length, and the decline is concentrated in rare classes and small objects.
cheapest_experiment: Extend one standard training run to 3x schedule with dense checkpointing, evaluate the trajectory; one long training run.

title: Domain randomization vs realism matching: which synthetic recipe wins where
problem: Synthetic-data practice assumes broad domain randomization beats effortful realism matching, but the comparison is rarely run at matched rendering budget for detection.
hypothesis: At matched rendering budget, realism-matched narrow synthetic data beats domain-randomized data when the target domain is known, and the reverse holds only when the target is unknown, quantifying the value of target knowledge.
cheapest_experiment: Render two matched synthetic sets (randomized vs matched to a chosen target camera), train identical detectors, test on the target; two renders plus two training runs.

title: Higher resolution does not help every class: per-class resolution sensitivity
problem: Resolution scaling is treated as a global knob, but classes with large context dependence may lose accuracy at higher resolution due to reduced receptive-field coverage.
hypothesis: A measurable subset of COCO classes has AP that decreases with input resolution, identifiable in advance by their context-dependence score.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 pretrained detectors at 5 input resolutions, plot per-class AP-vs-resolution; inference only.

title: Video pretraining for video detection: does temporal pretraining pay for itself
problem: It is assumed video tasks want video pretraining, but at matched compute, image pretraining plus temporal finetuning may dominate because image data is more diverse per FLOP.
hypothesis: At matched total pretraining compute, image-pretrained backbones finetuned with a lightweight temporal head match or beat video-pretrained backbones on video detection benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Compare public image-pretrained and video-pretrained backbones of matched scale under identical video-detection finetunes; two or three finetune runs.

title: Self-supervised vs supervised pretraining for dense tasks: a decontaminated comparison
problem: Claims that self-supervised pretraining transfers better to dense prediction often compare models differing in data, augmentation, and schedule simultaneously, so the causal factor is unidentified.
hypothesis: When data, augmentation, and compute are strictly matched, the dense-task advantage of self-supervised over supervised pretraining shrinks to near zero, indicating prior comparisons measured recipe differences.
cheapest_experiment: Pretrain two mid-size backbones (one SSL objective, one supervised) on identical data and schedule, finetune identical detectors; two pretraining runs at modest scale.

title: Augmentation gains do not transfer across detector families
problem: Augmentation policies validated on one detector family are assumed portable, but interaction effects between augmentation and matching/assignment strategies could break transfer.
hypothesis: The AP gain of a fixed augmentation policy varies in sign across detector families (anchor-based, anchor-free, query-based) trained on the same data.
cheapest_experiment: Cross 3 augmentation policies with 3 detector families in short-schedule runs; nine short training runs.

title: Detection does not need large batches: small-batch recipes revisited
problem: Large-batch training is assumed necessary for detection stability, an assumption inherited from BN-era recipes that may not survive modern normalization and optimizers.
hypothesis: With group normalization and appropriately scaled optimizers, batch-size-2 training reaches within noise of batch-size-32 results on COCO at matched total images seen.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs differing only in batch size and LR scaling; two training runs.

title: When does EMA hurt: mapping the EMA failure regime for detection
problem: Exponential moving average of weights is applied by default in modern detection recipes, but its interaction with short schedules and small datasets is assumed, not mapped.
hypothesis: EMA reduces final AP when the training schedule is short relative to the EMA horizon or when the dataset is small, with a predictable boundary in (schedule, decay) space.
cheapest_experiment: Grid of short training runs over schedule length and EMA decay on two dataset sizes; roughly 12 short runs.

title: Why mosaic works: scale jitter or context diversity
problem: Mosaic augmentation is credited with teaching context diversity, but its gains may reduce to the scale jitter it induces, which would let simpler pipelines replace it.
hypothesis: Matched scale-jitter augmentation without image compositing recovers the majority of mosaic's AP gain, and the residual is concentrated in no measurable stratum.
cheapest_experiment: Three matched training runs (no mosaic, mosaic, scale-jitter-matched) on one mid-size detector; three training runs.

title: Is deformable attention still necessary at modern scale
problem: Deformable attention was introduced to fix DETR convergence and small-object issues; whether modern training recipes and backbones have made it redundant is unexamined folklore.
hypothesis: With modern recipes, dense global attention matches deformable attention on COCO AP and small-object AP at matched wall-clock compute, removing the case for the added complexity.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs of one query-based detector with each attention type under a current recipe; two training runs.

title: Monocular depth cues are already inside detection features
problem: Detection pipelines are assumed depth-blind without dedicated sensors or heads, but backbone features may already encode coarse metric depth usable for free.
hypothesis: A frozen detection backbone supports linear-probe depth estimation at accuracy sufficient to order object pairs by distance above 80 percent, without any depth supervision during detection training.
cheapest_experiment: Linear-probe depth on frozen detector features using KITTI depth GT; probe training only.

title: Label smoothing in detection heads: calibration help or NMS poison
problem: Label smoothing is imported from classification into detection heads without examining its interaction with score-based suppression and ranking metrics.
hypothesis: Label smoothing compresses the score distribution in ways that degrade NMS separation of duplicates, lowering crowded-scene AP even when classification accuracy of matched boxes improves.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs with and without smoothing, evaluated on CrowdHuman and COCO with duplicate-analysis; two training runs.

title: Is COCO saturated, or are we measuring annotation errors: a residual-error census
problem: The belief that COCO is saturated assumes remaining errors are model errors; if most residual errors are annotation artifacts, the benchmark ended earlier than the community thinks.
hypothesis: Human adjudication of residual SOTA errors on COCO shows the majority are annotation problems (missing labels, wrong class, crowd mislabels) rather than genuine model failures.
cheapest_experiment: Sample 1,000 residual errors of a SOTA model, adjudicate with 2 annotators, classify error provenance; small annotation budget.

title: Are transformers really more robust than CNNs for dense prediction
problem: Transformer robustness claims come mostly from classification; whether they hold for detection and segmentation under matched pretraining and compute is assumed rather than shown.
hypothesis: At matched pretraining data and compute, transformer and CNN detectors show equal corruption robustness (relative AP drop on corrupted suites), localizing prior claims to pretraining differences.
cheapest_experiment: Finetune matched CNN and transformer backbones with identical heads, evaluate on corrupted COCO variants; two training runs plus corruption inference.

title: Distillation silently discards robustness: the hidden cost of student models
problem: Knowledge distillation is assumed to preserve what matters when compressing detectors, but robustness and calibration under shift may not transfer with clean AP.
hypothesis: Distilled detection students matching teachers within 1 clean AP lose disproportionately more AP under corruptions and domain shift, and the loss correlates with distillation temperature and feature-mimicking choices.
cheapest_experiment: Distill one student from one teacher under 3 recipes, evaluate all on corruption and cross-dataset suites; three distillation runs plus inference.

title: Test-time augmentation can hurt: mapping when TTA backfires
problem: TTA is assumed to be a free AP boost, but flip/scale averaging can distort score distributions and hurt rare classes and calibration in ways the headline number hides.
hypothesis: TTA improves pooled AP while degrading rare-class AP and post-hoc calibration for a measurable fraction of detectors, making it net harmful for threshold-based deployments.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 6 public detectors with and without standard TTA, stratify by class frequency and measure calibration; inference only.

title: Frozen BN folklore in small-batch finetuning: retest on modern stacks
problem: Freezing BatchNorm statistics during detection finetuning is inherited folklore from 2017-era recipes; whether it still matters with modern initialization and normalization is untested public knowledge.
hypothesis: On modern backbones, freezing vs updating BN statistics during finetuning changes final AP by less than seed noise, retiring a ritual that constrains recipe design.
cheapest_experiment: Four training runs (2 settings x 2 seeds) on one standard detector; four short runs.

title: Are larger models more label-efficient for detection specifically
problem: Label-efficiency scaling claims come from classification; detection has structured labels whose scaling behavior with model size may differ qualitatively.
hypothesis: The label-efficiency exponent (AP gain per doubling of labeled data) does not improve with model scale for detection finetuning, unlike classification, because localization supervision saturates differently.
cheapest_experiment: Train 3 model scales on 4 data fractions of COCO with fixed recipes, fit scaling curves; twelve short training runs.

title: Pretrain-finetune resolution matching: how much does it really matter
problem: The assumed need to match pretraining and finetuning resolution constrains recipe design, but its actual cost for dense tasks has not been isolated from confounds.
hypothesis: Resolution mismatch between pretraining and detection finetuning costs under 1 AP once positional embeddings are properly interpolated, making the matching folklore obsolete.
cheapest_experiment: Finetune one backbone pretrained at 3 resolutions onto a fixed detection resolution with proper interpolation; three training runs.

title: Do open-vocab detectors dominate closed-set specialists on their own turf
problem: The narrative says open-vocab models subsume closed-set detectors, but deployment users care about the gap on a fixed vocabulary and distribution, where specialists may still win at a fraction of the cost.
hypothesis: On fixed-vocabulary deployment-style test sets, compute-matched closed-set specialists beat open-vocab models by a stable margin that has not shrunk across recent open-vocab generations.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 generations of open-vocab models and matched closed-set baselines on 5 fixed-vocabulary datasets; inference plus a few finetunes.

title: SAM pseudo-masks as training data: characterizing the noise ceiling
problem: Auto-labeling with SAM-style models is assumed good enough to train segmentation students, but the structure of its errors (systematic boundary bias, part-whole confusion) may impose a hard student ceiling.
hypothesis: Students trained on SAM pseudo-masks plateau below students trained on human masks even with unlimited pseudo-labeled data, because pseudo-label errors are systematic rather than random.
cheapest_experiment: Train students on increasing volumes of pseudo-masks vs a fixed human-mask baseline on one domain, extrapolate the plateau; four training runs.

title: VLM benchmark scores do not predict grounding: captioning vs detection dissociation
problem: Model cards imply that better VQA/captioning VLMs ground language in space better, but grounding may dissociate from language-benchmark quality entirely.
hypothesis: Across 10 VLMs, referring-expression localization accuracy is uncorrelated with VQA/caption benchmark scores once model scale is controlled.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate public VLMs on RefCOCO-style grounding vs their published language scores, partial-correlate against parameter count; inference only.

title: Was hard negative mining actually made obsolete by focal loss
problem: The community retired explicit hard-negative mining after focal loss, but the equivalence was shown in balanced regimes; in long-tail and small-data regimes the retirement may be premature.
hypothesis: In long-tail detection, explicit hard-negative mining on top of focal loss improves tail AP beyond focal loss alone, contradicting the assumed subsumption.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs on LVIS (focal only vs focal plus mining); two training runs.

title: Multi-task learning with segmentation and depth: measuring interference honestly
problem: Multi-task training is assumed synergistic for dense tasks, but reported synergies rarely control for the extra supervision and compute the auxiliary tasks bring.
hypothesis: At strictly matched compute and annotation budget, adding segmentation or depth auxiliaries to detection training yields zero or negative AP change, revealing published synergies as budget artifacts.
cheapest_experiment: Three matched-budget runs (detection only, plus segmentation, plus depth) on one dataset with all budgets equalized; three training runs.

title: Resolution scaling vs model scaling for small objects: the real exchange rate
problem: Practitioners assume raising resolution is the best lever for small objects, but the exchange rate between resolution FLOPs and model-capacity FLOPs for small-object AP has not been published as a curve.
hypothesis: At matched inference FLOPs, allocating compute to resolution beats allocating to model width for small objects only below a resolution threshold, after which model scaling dominates.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate a FLOP-matched grid (3 resolutions x 3 model widths) with short finetunes on VisDrone; nine short runs.

title: Does crop augmentation teach translation equivariance, or do we just believe it does
problem: Random cropping is assumed to instill translation robustness in detectors, but learned equivariance has rarely been measured directly at the feature and prediction level.
hypothesis: Detectors trained with and without crop augmentation show indistinguishable prediction equivariance under sub-stride translations, because equivariance is dominated by architecture, not augmentation.
cheapest_experiment: Train two matched models, measure prediction drift under controlled pixel shifts; two short training runs plus analysis.

title: Is the syn2real gap mostly texture: a shape-texture decomposition for detection
problem: The texture-bias story from classification is assumed to explain the synthetic-to-real detection gap, but detection involves localization signals that may not follow classification-derived conclusions.
hypothesis: Style-transferring synthetic training images to real texture closes under half of the syn2real detection gap, showing the dominant gap components are geometric and distributional, not textural.
cheapest_experiment: Train on synthetic, texture-stylized synthetic, and real data; compare gaps on a real test set; three training runs on existing sim datasets.

title: Does CLIP robustness survive a detection head: robustness inheritance audit
problem: Zero-shot CLIP robustness under distribution shift is assumed to transfer to detection systems built on CLIP features, but heads and finetuning may destroy exactly the robust directions.
hypothesis: Detection heads finetuned on CLIP backbones lose most of the backbone's effective-robustness advantage relative to supervised backbones, measurable as the gap between zero-shot classification robustness and detection robustness under matched shifts.
cheapest_experiment: Compare effective robustness of CLIP-based vs supervised-based detectors on shifted detection sets, holding heads and data fixed; two finetunes plus inference.

title: Annotation quality vs quantity at fixed budget: the detection labeling exchange rate
problem: Teams assume annotation noise washes out at scale, but the exchange rate between label quality and quantity for detection at fixed labeling budget is unmeasured, leaving budget decisions to intuition.
hypothesis: At fixed annotation budget, a smaller carefully-verified dataset beats a larger single-pass dataset for detection AP whenever single-pass box-error rates exceed a threshold identifiable in advance from annotator agreement statistics.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate budget splits by degrading COCO labels at measured error rates vs subsampling, train matched detectors on each; four training runs.

title: Detectors that see ghosts: hallucinated detections of removed objects
problem: If detectors fire on context alone, they will detect objects that have been physically removed from a scene, a phenomenon with direct safety consequences that lacks systematic measurement.
hypothesis: After high-quality inpainting removal of an object, standard detectors still detect the removed object above deployment thresholds in a substantial fraction of cases, and the ghost rate correlates with class-context strength.
cheapest_experiment: Inpaint 1,000 object instances out of COCO images, run 5 detectors, measure ghost-detection rates per class; inpainting plus inference.

title: Compression fingerprints: does re-encoding test images toward the training distribution raise AP
problem: Models may key on JPEG/codec fingerprints of their training corpus; if re-encoding test images with training-matched settings changes AP, benchmarks partially measure codec matching.
hypothesis: Re-encoding test images to match training-set compression statistics increases AP measurably for models trained on heavily web-scraped data, and the effect disappears for models trained on raw-captured data.
cheapest_experiment: Re-encode COCO val under several codec settings, evaluate a panel of detectors, correlate AP shifts with training-data provenance; inference only.
notes: UNVERIFIED - needs lit search on codec-bias studies for detection.

title: How far do random features go: detection with frozen random backbones
problem: The baseline of a frozen randomly-initialized backbone with a trained detection head is almost never reported, so the community cannot say how much of detection performance comes from learned representations versus architectural priors and head capacity.
hypothesis: A frozen random backbone with a trained head achieves a nontrivial fraction of pretrained AP (operationally, over a third on COCO), and the fraction grows with head capacity, revealing substantial architectural prior.
cheapest_experiment: Train heads on frozen random vs frozen pretrained backbones at two head capacities; four short training runs.

title: Rank stability under benign transforms predicts AP without labels
problem: Estimating detector quality on unlabeled deployment data is an open problem; the stability of confidence rankings under label-preserving transforms might be a free, label-less quality signal.
hypothesis: The rank correlation of detection confidences across benign transforms (small shifts, mild color jitter) of the same images predicts held-out AP across models and domains with correlation above 0.8.
cheapest_experiment: Compute the stability statistic and true AP for 10 models across 5 datasets; inference only.

title: Class frequency as a feature: balanced training can hurt balanced testing
problem: Class rebalancing assumes natural frequency is a nuisance, but frequency priors may be genuine signal that detectors exploit even on balanced test sets via context correlations.
hypothesis: Detectors trained on natural class frequencies outperform frequency-balanced training even on class-balanced test sets, because frequency correlates with informative context statistics.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs (natural vs balanced sampling) evaluated on balanced and natural test splits; two training runs.

title: Action at a distance: local perturbations flip detections elsewhere in the image
problem: Detection pipelines couple predictions through shared features and NMS, so a small local perturbation might flip detections far away, a nonlocality that has safety implications and no systematic characterization.
hypothesis: Optimized small patches confined to background regions can suppress or create detections at distances beyond any receptive-field overlap, and the effect operates primarily through score-ranking interactions in suppression.
cheapest_experiment: Run patch optimization against 2 detectors with NMS on 100 images, ablate the effect with NMS removed; small adversarial-optimization compute.

title: Train-test duplication in detection benchmarks: a contamination census
problem: Near-duplicate images across train and test splits inflate benchmark scores, and no recent audit quantifies this for major detection datasets and web-pretrained models.
hypothesis: Perceptual-hash and embedding-based auditing finds a nonzero contamination rate in popular detection benchmarks, and models score measurably higher on contaminated test images than on matched clean ones.
cheapest_experiment: Run duplicate detection between train/test of 3 benchmarks and between web-pretraining corpora and test sets where feasible, compare per-image AP on flagged vs clean subsets; analysis only.

title: Does double descent exist for dense prediction
problem: Double descent is documented for classification, but detection couples classification with regression and matching, and whether the phenomenon appears in dense tasks is unknown.
hypothesis: COCO AP as a function of model width exhibits a measurable non-monotonic region near the interpolation threshold of the classification subtask, i.e. double descent survives task compositionality.
cheapest_experiment: Train a width ladder (8 widths) of a small detector on a subsampled dataset to reach interpolation; eight small training runs.

title: Vocabulary ordering effects in open-vocab detectors
problem: Open-vocab detectors consume class lists whose ordering should be irrelevant, yet tokenization, truncation, and attention position effects may make output depend on class order.
