hypothesis: Permuting the inference vocabulary order changes per-class AP beyond numerical noise for at least some open-vocab architectures, revealing an unphysical sensitivity.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 open-vocab detectors under 10 random vocabulary permutations on COCO; inference only.

title: Boxes snap to the stride grid: quantization artifacts in outputs
problem: Detector box coordinates may cluster on the feature-stride grid, an artifact that inflates or deflates IoU systematically at small scales and has never been measured across architectures.
hypothesis: Output box coordinates show significant spectral peaks at stride harmonics, the effect grows as object size shrinks, and grid-aware post-hoc decoding improves small-object AP for free.
cheapest_experiment: Fourier-analyze coordinate residuals of cached predictions from 6 detectors, then test a de-quantization correction; analysis only.

title: Canonical-orientation advantage survives rotation augmentation
problem: If detectors remain better at canonical orientations despite rotation augmentation, augmentation is not delivering the invariance the community assumes it buys.
hypothesis: Detectors trained with rotation augmentation still show a measurable AP advantage at canonical orientations for orientation-canonical classes, indicating augmentation reshapes but does not equalize the orientation prior.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate rotation-augmented public models on synthetically rotated test suites, plot AP vs rotation angle per class; inference only.

title: Early checkpoints are OOD-robust: the robustness-accuracy trade along training time
problem: If mid-training checkpoints are more robust under shift while worse in-distribution, checkpoint selection is silently choosing a robustness trade-off nobody is measuring.
hypothesis: Relative AP drop under corruption and cross-dataset shift decreases early in training and then worsens as in-distribution AP keeps rising, producing a robustness-optimal checkpoint distinct from the AP-optimal one.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate a dense checkpoint trajectory of one standard training run on clean and shifted suites; one training run with checkpointing plus inference.

title: Deleting the hardest training images can raise AP
problem: If a small fraction of training images (heavy noise, pathological annotations) hurts optimization, dataset pruning would beat dataset growth in some regimes, contradicting more-data instincts.
hypothesis: Removing the training images with highest per-image loss variance across seeds improves final COCO AP relative to training on the full set, and the removed set is enriched for annotation errors on inspection.
cheapest_experiment: Score training images by cross-seed loss variance from 2 cheap runs, retrain without the top 5 percent, compare; three training runs.

title: Ensemble disagreement is an annotation-error detector
problem: Auditing datasets for annotation errors is expensive; if model committees disagree precisely where labels are wrong, disagreement is a free auditing signal with measurable precision.
hypothesis: Instances where a diverse detector ensemble agrees with each other but disagrees with GT are enriched for annotation errors at a precision above 70 percent, validated by human adjudication.
cheapest_experiment: Rank COCO val GT instances by ensemble-vs-GT disagreement, human-verify the top 300; inference plus small annotation.

title: White balance flips classes: color constancy failures in detection
problem: Detectors may rely on absolute color in ways that break under plausible white-balance shifts, a failure mode invisible in standard benchmarks captured under favorable processing.
hypothesis: Physically plausible white-balance shifts (within camera-realistic ranges) change predicted classes for a measurable fraction of instances, concentrated in color-diagnostic categories.
cheapest_experiment: Apply camera-calibrated white-balance transforms to COCO val, measure class-flip rates per category for 4 detectors; inference only.

title: Training with box jitter improves calibration for free
problem: Annotation noise is usually treated as harm, but injecting controlled box jitter during training might act as a calibration regularizer without hurting AP, which would be a cheap deployment win.
hypothesis: Training with small random box jitter yields detectors with measurably better confidence-IoU calibration at unchanged AP, across two architectures.
cheapest_experiment: Four training runs (2 architectures x jitter on/off), measure AP and spatial calibration; four short runs.

title: Batch composition effects: who shares your batch changes what you learn
problem: With batch-dependent statistics and loss normalization, the semantic composition of batches could have lasting effects on detection training beyond learning-rate schedules, an untested source of irreproducibility.
hypothesis: Controlling batch composition (semantically clustered vs dispersed batches) at fixed data and schedule changes final AP beyond seed noise, revealing an unmanaged training hyperparameter.
cheapest_experiment: Three training runs with different batch-composition policies plus seed replicates on a small detector; six short runs.

title: Typographic hijacking of open-vocab detectors by scene text
problem: Open-vocab detectors couple image regions to text embeddings, so written words in the scene may hijack detections (a sticker saying banana on a stop sign), a deployment-relevant confusion channel that is unmeasured at detection granularity.
hypothesis: Inserting printed class names into scenes creates false detections of those classes localized on the text region at rates far above matched non-word textures, for multiple open-vocab architectures.
cheapest_experiment: Paste rendered words vs matched scrambled-letter controls into 500 images, compare false-fire rates; compositing plus inference.

title: Asymmetric cross-dataset generalization: why does A beat B transfer to B but not vice versa
problem: Cross-dataset transfer between similar detection datasets is often strongly asymmetric, and the field lacks a validated explanation (diversity, label style, image quality) for the direction of the arrow.
hypothesis: Transfer asymmetry between dataset pairs is predicted by a label-convention divergence measure and not by raw dataset size or image diversity, isolating annotation style as the causal factor.
cheapest_experiment: Cross-train and cross-test small detectors over 4 dataset pairs, regress asymmetry on candidate factors; eight short training runs.

title: Co-occurrence overrides appearance: keyboard detected beside monitor-shaped blobs
problem: Detectors may fire on contextual configurations rather than object appearance, so an appearance-free blob in a canonical context could be detected as the expected object, quantifying context dominance.
hypothesis: Replacing an object with a shape-matched featureless blob preserves detection of its usual co-occurring partner classes at high confidence, and even yields detection of the blob itself as the expected class in a measurable fraction of scenes.
cheapest_experiment: Blob-substitute 500 instances from strong co-occurrence pairs, run 4 detectors, measure context-driven detection rates; compositing plus inference.

title: Seed variance vs published deltas: how much of the leaderboard is luck
problem: Detection papers rarely report seed variance, so the community cannot tell what fraction of claimed improvements exceed run-to-run noise, a foundational measurement that is simply missing at scale.
hypothesis: The cross-seed standard deviation of COCO AP for standard recipes is large enough that a substantial fraction of published year-over-year improvements fall within two standard deviations of seed noise.
cheapest_experiment: Train 10 seeds each of 3 standard recipes, publish the variance components, compare with a curated list of published deltas; thirty short-to-medium runs, the single most reusable dataset this cluster could produce.

title: The interpolation-kernel hyperparameter nobody reports
problem: Image resize kernels (bilinear, bicubic, area, antialias flags) differ across frameworks and are rarely reported, yet they change small-object statistics and may shift AP measurably.
hypothesis: Switching resize kernels between common defaults changes COCO AP-small by amounts comparable to published method improvements, and mismatched train-test kernels cause a further systematic drop.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 5 pretrained detectors under a grid of test-time resize kernels, and finetune one model under two kernels; mostly inference plus two short runs.

title: Dataset-of-origin is readable from local patches: fingerprints and their leakage
problem: If small patches suffice to classify which dataset an image came from, detectors can exploit dataset fingerprints as shortcuts, undermining cross-dataset conclusions in ways quantifiable by patch classifiers.
hypothesis: A shallow classifier on 32x32 patches distinguishes major detection datasets far above chance, and detector features trained on those datasets encode the same fingerprint dimensions, measurable by probing.
cheapest_experiment: Train a patch classifier across 4 datasets, probe detector features for fingerprint recoverability; small training runs.

title: NMS destroys usable ranking information: pre-suppression logits know more
problem: Suppression discards nearly-duplicate candidates whose scores collectively carry information about localization uncertainty and ranking quality that single surviving boxes lack.
hypothesis: A post-hoc re-scorer using pre-NMS candidate sets (score distributions over duplicates) improves final AP and calibration over standard NMS output without retraining, proving suppression loses recoverable information.
cheapest_experiment: Implement candidate-set re-scoring on cached pre-NMS outputs of 3 detectors; analysis only.

title: Partial freezing beats full finetuning: mapping implicit regularization
problem: Occasional reports that freezing random weight subsets improves transfer suggest an unmapped implicit-regularization effect that could deliver free gains in detection finetuning.
hypothesis: For detection finetuning on small datasets, freezing a random fraction of backbone parameters outperforms full finetuning, with an optimal freeze fraction that grows as the dataset shrinks.
cheapest_experiment: Grid over freeze fractions on 3 dataset sizes with one detector; twelve short runs.

title: Border effects: padding values leak into detections at image edges
problem: Zero-padding and letterboxing conventions create artificial statistics at image borders that may systematically distort detections near edges, an artifact never audited across architectures.
hypothesis: Detection recall and box accuracy degrade within a boundary band whose width matches the receptive-field halo of padding, and replacing zero-padding with reflective padding at inference shifts detections measurably without retraining.
cheapest_experiment: Compare edge-band vs interior AP on cached predictions, then re-run inference with altered padding for 3 detectors; inference only.

title: Semantic instability of class names: person vs human vs pedestrian
problem: Open-vocab systems treat class-name choice as a detail, but near-synonymous names may produce materially different detectors, meaning reported numbers are name-conditional in an unreported way.
hypothesis: AP for the same visual category varies by several points across near-synonymous prompt names, and the best name differs across architectures, making single-name evaluation misleading.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 open-vocab detectors under 8 synonym sets on COCO categories; inference only.

title: Left-right asymmetry: photographer bias becomes model bias
problem: Human photos have systematic left-right composition biases; if detectors inherit them, horizontal flips at test time should change results in structured ways that reveal learned spatial priors.
hypothesis: Per-class AP differs measurably between original and mirrored test sets for classes with strong composition biases, and the asymmetry correlates with position statistics in training data.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 5 detectors on flipped COCO val, correlate per-class asymmetry with train position statistics; inference only.

title: Mixed precision changes small-object results beyond noise
problem: AMP is assumed numerically innocuous, but small objects live in low-magnitude feature regimes where reduced precision could bite, and nobody has isolated this effect for detection.
hypothesis: Training and inference precision changes (FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16) shift AP-small beyond cross-seed noise while leaving AP-large unchanged, revealing a precision-sensitivity gradient with object size.
cheapest_experiment: Six runs (3 precisions x 2 seeds) of one detector, plus precision-swapped inference on fixed checkpoints; six short runs.

title: Vocabulary interference: longer class lists degrade detection of the same classes
problem: Open-vocab detection quality on a fixed target class may depend on what else is in the query vocabulary, an interference effect with direct API-design consequences that is unquantified.
hypothesis: AP on a fixed set of target classes decreases monotonically as unrelated distractor classes are added to the inference vocabulary, and the decay rate differs enough across architectures to change model choice for large-vocabulary applications.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 3 open-vocab detectors on fixed targets with vocabulary sizes from 10 to 5,000; inference only.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Attention maps fail sanity checks as detection explanations
problem: Attention visualizations are routinely presented as explanations of detection decisions; if they fail randomization and deletion sanity checks, a large body of interpretability practice in detection is invalid.
hypothesis: Attention-based explanation maps for detections are insensitive to randomization of late-layer weights and their high-attention regions are not causally necessary (deletion barely changes the detection), failing both standard sanity checks.
cheapest_experiment: Apply weight-randomization and deletion tests to attention explanations of 3 detection transformers on 200 detections; inference-scale compute.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Web-scale pretraining saturates for detection: the flat tail of the data curve
problem: The assumption that another order of magnitude of pretraining data will lift dense-task transfer keeps enormous scraping efforts alive; a measured saturation point would redirect that effort.
hypothesis: Detection finetuning AP as a function of pretraining corpus size is flat within noise beyond a corpus size achievable at academic scale, for fixed model capacity.
cheapest_experiment: Use public checkpoint families pretrained on nested data scales, finetune identical detection heads, plot the curve; several finetunes only.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Video architectures vs frame detector plus tracker: an equal-compute showdown
problem: Dedicated video detection architectures are compared against weak frame baselines; if a strong frame detector plus a trivial temporal smoother wins at equal compute, the subfield needs redirection.
hypothesis: At matched total inference FLOPs, a strong single-frame detector with score smoothing along tracks matches or beats dedicated video detection architectures on standard benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Tune a frame-detector-plus-smoother pipeline at the FLOP budget of 2 video architectures, compare on ImageNet-VID and OVIS; inference plus light tuning.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Uncertainty methods do not improve detection decisions at matched cost
problem: MC dropout and deep ensembles are promoted for detection UQ, but if their decision-utility gain disappears once compute is matched against simply using a bigger or better-calibrated single model, current UQ practice is misallocated compute.
hypothesis: At matched inference compute, a single larger detector with post-hoc calibration achieves equal or better risk-coverage utility than MC-dropout or ensemble UQ on the same architecture family.
cheapest_experiment: Compare risk-coverage curves of ensemble/MC variants vs compute-matched single models on COCO and a shifted set; inference plus calibration fitting.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Domain adaptation for detection loses to 50 labeled target images
problem: Unsupervised domain adaptation methods for detection claim to avoid target labeling, but if a trivial finetune on a tiny labeled target set dominates them, the practical case for UDA collapses for most applications.
hypothesis: Finetuning on 50 labeled target-domain images beats published unsupervised adaptation methods on standard detection UDA benchmarks, at a labeling cost under one annotator-day.
cheapest_experiment: Label-budgeted finetunes vs public UDA results on 3 standard benchmark pairs; a few short finetunes.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Curriculum learning does nothing for detection: a preregistered replication
problem: Curriculum strategies keep being proposed for detection without a preregistered, seed-replicated null test; establishing the null would save the community recurring effort.
hypothesis: Across easy-to-hard curricula defined by object size, count, and loss, no curriculum beats shuffled training beyond seed noise on COCO at matched compute.
cheapest_experiment: Preregister analysis, run 3 curricula x 3 seeds vs 3 shuffled seeds on one detector; nine short runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Learned augmentation policies for detection: no transfer, no gain
problem: AutoAugment-style searched policies for detection are expensive and assumed portable; a demonstration that they neither transfer across datasets nor beat simple jitter would retire a costly practice.
hypothesis: Searched augmentation policies transferred across detection datasets perform no better than a two-parameter scale-color jitter baseline at matched training compute.
cheapest_experiment: Train with transferred searched policies vs simple jitter on 2 datasets and 2 detectors; eight short runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: FPN variants under equal tuning: does neck research replicate
problem: Successive neck designs (path aggregation, bidirectional fusion) claim steady gains over FPN, but the baselines were rarely given equal tuning budgets, casting doubt on the cumulative story.
hypothesis: Under equal hyperparameter search budgets, modern neck variants provide no significant AP gain over a well-tuned FPN across two detector families.
cheapest_experiment: Matched search-budget tuning of FPN vs 2 modern necks on 2 detectors; a bounded tuning grid of short runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Self-training gains evaporate when the confidence threshold is honestly chosen
problem: Semi-supervised detection pipelines tune pseudo-label thresholds on labeled validation data from the target distribution, a subtle leakage that may account for much of the reported gains.
hypothesis: When pseudo-label thresholds are chosen without target-distribution validation access (transferred from a disjoint dataset), published self-training gains shrink by more than half.
cheapest_experiment: Re-run 2 public semi-supervised detection methods with honestly transferred thresholds; a few training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: SAM auto-labels cap student quality in crowded scenes
problem: Auto-labeling pipelines using promptable segmenters are replacing human annotation, but in crowded scenes their systematic merge/split errors may impose a hard ceiling on trainable student quality.
hypothesis: Students trained on promptable-model auto-labels of crowded scenes plateau below 80 percent of the human-label student AP regardless of auto-label volume, because merge/split errors are systematic.
cheapest_experiment: Train students on increasing auto-label volumes vs human labels on CrowdHuman; four training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Synthetic pretraining gains vanish under a properly tuned real-data schedule
problem: Papers report synthetic pretraining boosts for detection against real-data baselines with default schedules; if tuning the baseline erases the boost, the synthetic-pretraining literature needs re-founding.
hypothesis: After tuning the real-data-only schedule (longer training, better LR), the AP advantage of synthetic pretraining drops to within seed noise on standard syn2real detection setups.
cheapest_experiment: Tune the real-only baseline with a bounded budget, compare against published synthetic-pretraining results; several short runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Distilling open-vocab teachers loses exactly the rare classes
problem: Distillation of open-vocab teachers into fast students is the standard deployment path, but the distillation objective may transfer head-class behavior while discarding the rare-class ability that motivated open-vocab in the first place.
hypothesis: Distilled students retain head-class AP within 1 point of teachers while losing a disproportionate share of tail-class AP, and the loss is not repaired by rebalancing the distillation data.
cheapest_experiment: Distill one open-vocab teacher under 2 data-balance regimes, evaluate frequency-stratified AP; two distillation runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Temperature scaling does not survive NMS: post-processing breaks calibration
problem: Calibration is typically applied to raw scores before suppression, but NMS selects extreme order statistics, which re-distorts calibrated probabilities; if standard recipes fail, detection calibration practice must move post-NMS.
hypothesis: Temperature scaling fitted pre-NMS leaves post-NMS outputs materially miscalibrated (selection bias of maxima), while fitting calibration on post-NMS survivors fixes it, across architectures.
cheapest_experiment: Fit and evaluate calibration at both pipeline stages for 4 detectors on COCO; analysis only.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Active learning for detection fails at realistic batch sizes: a multi-codebase replication
problem: Active learning papers report gains with small acquisition batches and single codebases; practitioners use large batches, where diversity effects may reduce AL to random sampling.
hypothesis: At acquisition batches of 5,000-plus images, no published detection AL method beats random sampling beyond seed noise, replicated across two codebases and two datasets.
cheapest_experiment: Run 3 AL methods vs random at large batch on 2 datasets with 2 seeds; a bounded set of short training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: CAM-style weak localization does not beat gradient-norm baselines
problem: A stream of weakly-supervised localization methods builds on class-activation mapping; if trivial gradient-magnitude baselines match them under fair evaluation, the methodological premise needs revision.
hypothesis: Under a shared evaluation protocol with matched backbones, simple input-gradient-norm maps localize objects as well as CAM descendants on standard weak-localization benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 5 methods and the gradient baseline on CUB/ImageNet localization with one backbone; inference only.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Test-time adaptation collapses under continual shift for detection
problem: Entropy-minimization TTA methods are being ported to detection; their error-accumulation behavior under long, drifting deployment streams may make them worse than frozen models, which practitioners need to know before adoption.
hypothesis: Under continual shift sequences longer than a few thousand frames, current TTA methods degrade below the frozen-model baseline for detection, with collapse onset predictable from update-rate settings.
cheapest_experiment: Run 2 TTA methods vs frozen baseline over long corrupted video streams, track AP over time; inference-scale compute.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Adversarial training buys less than it costs for deployed detectors
problem: Adversarial training for detection sacrifices clean AP for robustness against threat models rarely realized in deployments; an honest cost-benefit accounting could redirect robustness effort toward realistic corruptions.
hypothesis: Under a deployment threat model of physical and compression perturbations (not norm-bounded attacks), adversarially trained detectors are dominated by corruption-augmented training at every point of the clean-robust trade-off curve.
cheapest_experiment: Train both variants at matched compute, evaluate on physical-style and corruption suites; two training runs plus inference.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Bigger vocabularies hurt base classes: negative transfer in open-vocab training
problem: Scaling training vocabularies is assumed harmless for existing classes, but embedding-space crowding may degrade base-class detection, a trade-off that changes how vocabularies should be grown.
hypothesis: Increasing training vocabulary size at fixed data and compute monotonically decreases base-class AP beyond a vocabulary threshold, demonstrating negative transfer within open-vocab training.
cheapest_experiment: Train one open-vocab detector at 4 vocabulary scales with fixed images, track base-class AP; four training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Mask refinement modules polish metrics, not measurements
problem: Boundary-refinement modules improve mask metrics, but downstream scientific uses (cell area, lesion volume) depend on unbiased measurement; refinement may improve IoU while biasing area estimates.
hypothesis: Refinement modules that raise mask AP leave downstream area-estimation bias unchanged or worse, because they optimize boundary placement toward annotation style rather than physical truth.
cheapest_experiment: Compare area-estimation bias against high-precision GT (calibrated microscopy set) with and without refinement modules; inference only.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Depth-aware detection heads die by estimated depth
problem: Methods injecting depth into detection assume depth is available; with estimated monocular depth, error propagation may cancel the benefit entirely, which determines whether the approach is deployable without depth sensors.
hypothesis: Detection gains from GT-depth injection disappear or invert when depth is replaced by monocular estimates, across two depth-aware architectures.
cheapest_experiment: Swap GT depth for estimated depth in 2 public depth-aware detectors, compare AP; inference plus light finetuning.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Few-shot detection methods vs a strong finetuning baseline
problem: Few-shot detection methods are compared against weak finetuning baselines; if modern augmentation and schedules make plain finetuning win, the specialized-methods literature loses its motivation.
hypothesis: Full-detector finetuning with strong augmentation on the few shots beats published few-shot detection methods on standard splits at matched compute.
cheapest_experiment: Tune the finetuning baseline once, run over standard episodes vs published numbers; light finetune compute.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Positional-encoding variants for detection transformers: a null at scale
problem: A stream of positional-encoding proposals for detection transformers reports small gains at small scale; testing whether any survive at modern scale would prune the design space for everyone.
hypothesis: At current-standard model and data scale, positional-encoding variants for detection transformers differ by less than seed noise in final AP.
cheapest_experiment: Train 4 encoding variants x 2 seeds at one modern scale; eight training runs, expensive but decisive.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Loss reweighting equals resampling for long-tail detection
problem: Long-tail detection papers propose increasingly complex loss reweighting schemes; if simple resampling matches them all in matched setups, the complexity is unjustified.
hypothesis: Under matched compute and tuning budgets, no published reweighting scheme beats class-frequency resampling on LVIS beyond seed noise.
cheapest_experiment: Re-run 3 reweighting schemes and resampling under one shared recipe with 2 seeds each; eight short runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Semi-supervised detection dies on truly out-of-distribution unlabeled data
problem: Semi-supervised detection is benchmarked with unlabeled data drawn from the labeled distribution, but real unlabeled pools are OOD; measuring the gain collapse under honest pools would reset expectations.
hypothesis: When the unlabeled pool comes from a different distribution than the labeled set, semi-supervised detection gains shrink to noise or become negative, across two representative methods.
cheapest_experiment: Re-run 2 methods with OOD unlabeled pools (different dataset as pool); a few training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Why model soups fail for detection heads
problem: Weight averaging (soups) works for classification finetunes but is anecdotally unreliable for detection; establishing and explaining the failure would prevent wasted adoption and might reveal loss-landscape structure specific to dense heads.
hypothesis: Averaging independently finetuned detection models damages AP whenever the heads involve matching-dependent losses, and the damage localizes to the head layers (backbone-only averaging still works).
cheapest_experiment: Finetune 4 runs, evaluate full-soup vs backbone-only-soup vs individuals; four short runs plus evaluation.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: NAS-found detection architectures do not transfer across datasets
problem: Neural architecture search for detection reports wins on the search dataset; if found architectures underperform hand-designed ones off-dataset, the search is overfitting and the practice needs course correction.
hypothesis: Architectures searched on one detection dataset lose their advantage (or invert) when trained from scratch on a different dataset, across two published NAS results.
cheapest_experiment: Retrain 2 NAS-found and 2 baseline architectures on a held-out dataset; four training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Region-contrastive pretraining does not beat plain supervised pretraining, compute-matched
problem: Dense/region-level contrastive pretraining methods claim detection-specific transfer advantages, but comparisons rarely match total pretraining compute against strong supervised recipes.
hypothesis: At matched pretraining compute and data, region-contrastive objectives provide no detection finetuning advantage over modern supervised pretraining.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched pretrainings at modest scale plus identical finetunes; two pretraining runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Saliency explanations fail the deletion test for detection
problem: Deletion-based evaluation of explanations exists for classification; applying it rigorously to detection explanations would test whether any current method identifies causally relevant pixels for localization decisions.
hypothesis: For all tested explanation methods, deleting the top-ranked pixels changes detections less than deleting random pixels of matched area from within the box, failing causal validity for localization.
cheapest_experiment: Run deletion curves for 4 explanation methods over 300 detections and 3 detectors; inference-scale compute.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Progressive resizing and multi-stage recipes: no benefit at matched compute
problem: Multi-stage training recipes (small-to-large resolution) persist in practice without controlled evidence at matched total compute; a decisive null would simplify pipelines everywhere.
hypothesis: At matched total training FLOPs, progressive-resolution schedules match but do not beat single-resolution training on final COCO AP.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched-FLOP training runs per architecture on 2 architectures; four training runs.

cluster: Negative results that would change practice
title: Auxiliary geometric tasks do not help detection at matched budgets
problem: Auxiliary depth/normal/edge prediction heads are claimed to improve detection through richer representations; matched-budget accounting (the auxiliary labels and compute could buy more detection data) is missing.
hypothesis: When the budget spent on auxiliary supervision is converted into additional detection data or training length, plain detection training dominates auxiliary multi-task training.
cheapest_experiment: Three matched-budget runs (aux-task, longer training, more data) on one dataset; three training runs.

title: One temperature does not fit all classes: class-conditional calibration structure
problem: Detector calibration is corrected globally, but per-class score distributions differ so much that global calibration may leave every individual class miscalibrated in opposite directions.
hypothesis: Class-conditional recalibration reduces deployment decision cost substantially over global calibration, and the per-class temperature correlates with class frequency and intra-class appearance variance.
cheapest_experiment: Fit global vs per-class calibrators on cached predictions of 5 detectors, compare expected cost on held-out data; analysis only.

title: Confidence should predict IoU: spatial calibration as a first-class metric
problem: Detection confidence is treated as existence probability, but users read it as overall quality including localization; the actual confidence-IoU relationship is weak and unreported.
hypothesis: For most detectors, confidence explains under a quarter of the variance in matched-detection IoU, and adding a cheap IoU-prediction head fixes this without AP cost, changing downstream filtering quality materially.
cheapest_experiment: Measure confidence-IoU correlation on cached predictions of 8 detectors, finetune one IoU head; analysis plus one short finetune.

title: Synthetic corruptions do not predict real degradation: a paired-camera study
problem: Corruption benchmarks apply synthetic noise/blur/weather to clean images; whether robustness rankings on them predict rankings on genuinely degraded captures is the load-bearing assumption of the whole robustness literature.
hypothesis: Detector robustness rankings on synthetic corruption suites correlate poorly with rankings on paired real degraded captures (same scenes through real fog, low light, dirty optics).
cheapest_experiment: Collect a modest paired set (rig with two cameras, one degraded), evaluate 8 detectors on both, compare rank orders; small capture effort plus inference.

title: How to ensemble boxes: fusion rules change calibration more than accuracy
problem: Detection ensembling lacks a principled combination rule (score averaging, box fusion, union-NMS), and the choice may affect calibration and downstream utility more than raw AP, which is what papers report.
hypothesis: Across fusion rules, AP varies little but calibration and risk-coverage utility vary substantially, making fusion-rule choice a calibration decision misclassified as an accuracy decision.
cheapest_experiment: Implement 4 fusion rules over fixed ensemble members, evaluate AP, calibration, and risk-coverage; inference plus analysis.

title: Unknown objects get confident known labels: measuring open-set overclaiming
problem: Deployed detectors face objects outside their vocabulary and typically shoehorn them into known classes with high confidence; the rate of this overclaiming is a missing standard measurement.
hypothesis: On scenes containing out-of-vocabulary objects, standard detectors assign above-threshold known-class labels to a large fraction of them, and the overclaiming rate is uncorrelated with in-vocabulary AP, making it an independent model-selection axis.
cheapest_experiment: Build an out-of-vocabulary test set from LVIS-minus-COCO classes, measure overclaim rates of 6 COCO detectors; inference only.

title: Confidence should fall as occlusion grows: testing monotonicity
problem: A trustworthy detector should lower its confidence as evidence is progressively hidden, but confidence-vs-occlusion monotonicity has never been tested systematically and violations would matter for safety filtering.
hypothesis: Under progressive controlled occlusion of the same instance, detector confidence is non-monotonic for a substantial fraction of instances, including confidence increases as objects become more hidden.
cheapest_experiment: Progressively occlude 500 instances with sliding masks, log confidence trajectories for 5 detectors; compositing plus inference.

title: Detectors cannot abstain: risk-coverage as a standard detection report
problem: Selective prediction (abstaining on uncertain images or regions) is essential in deployment, yet detection benchmarks never report risk-coverage behavior, and detector scores may be poor abstention signals.
hypothesis: Image-level abstention driven by simple aggregates of detection scores leaves large fractions of achievable risk-coverage utility unrealized relative to an oracle, and the gap differs across detectors that share the same AP.
cheapest_experiment: Compute risk-coverage curves from cached predictions with several abstention scores for 8 detectors; analysis only.

title: Label-noise dose-response curves for detection losses
problem: Detection losses (focal, IoU-based, matching-based) have unknown relative sensitivity to annotation noise, so practitioners cannot choose losses based on their data quality.
hypothesis: Injecting controlled box-jitter and class-flip noise produces distinct dose-response curves per loss family, with matching-based losses degrading fastest under box noise.
cheapest_experiment: Train a small detector grid (3 losses x 4 noise doses) on a subsampled dataset; twelve short runs.

title: Real fog vs rendered fog: the atmospheric-model gap
problem: Fog robustness is trained and tested with scattering models applied to clear images; the residual gap to real fog determines whether simulation suffices, and it has not been isolated with matched scenes.
hypothesis: Detectors hardened on rendered fog recover only part of their AP loss on real fog, and the residual gap is dominated by illumination and contrast structure absent from standard scattering models.
cheapest_experiment: Use existing paired/comparable clear-fog datasets, evaluate fog-hardened vs baseline models on both fog types, decompose errors; inference only.

title: Do learned box variances mean anything: testing aleatoric UQ against controlled ambiguity
problem: Detectors with probabilistic box heads output variances that are used as uncertainty, but whether these variances track actual ambiguity (vs just object scale) has not been causally tested.
hypothesis: Learned box variances correlate primarily with object size and only weakly with controlled ambiguity (synthetic blur, occlusion of the same instance), failing as ambiguity meters.
cheapest_experiment: Manipulate ambiguity on fixed instances, log variance responses vs size controls for 2 probabilistic detectors; compositing plus inference.

title: Rare classes are overconfident: calibration under class imbalance
problem: Calibration analyses pool classes, hiding that tail classes may be systematically overconfident because their scores were shaped by few positives, which corrupts threshold transfer to rare categories.
hypothesis: Calibration error grows monotonically as class frequency falls, and frequency-aware calibration transfers thresholds to unseen rare classes better than global calibration.
cheapest_experiment: Stratify calibration by class frequency on LVIS predictions of 4 detectors, fit and test frequency-aware calibrators; analysis only.

title: Focal length and distortion sweeps: detection robustness to camera intrinsics
problem: Deployment cameras differ from benchmark cameras in intrinsics (focal length, distortion), and detector sensitivity to these parameters is unmeasured because benchmarks fix them implicitly.
hypothesis: Re-rendering test images under swept intrinsics produces AP degradation curves steep enough that intrinsics mismatch explains a meaningful share of reported cross-dataset gaps.
cheapest_experiment: Warp COCO val under parameterized intrinsics changes, evaluate 5 detectors, then compare against actual cross-dataset gaps; inference only.

title: Multi-view consistency as a free robustness audit
problem: Multi-camera rigs see the same objects from several views; per-object detection consistency across views is a label-free robustness signal that could audit deployed systems continuously, but its relationship to accuracy is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Cross-view detection inconsistency rate correlates strongly with single-view AP measured against labels, enabling label-free monitoring within a stated error band.
cheapest_experiment: Use existing multi-view datasets (nuScenes, Waymo) to compute consistency vs labeled AP across 6 detectors; analysis only.

title: Universal patch vulnerability: transfer structure across detector families
problem: Adversarial patches are studied per-model; whether a shared vulnerability subspace exists across architectures determines whether patch defense is a per-model or ecosystem problem.
hypothesis: Patches optimized jointly on two detector families transfer to unseen families with attack success above 50 percent, indicating a shared vulnerability structure rooted in low-level feature statistics.
cheapest_experiment: Optimize patches on 2 families, test on 4 held-out detectors; bounded adversarial-optimization compute.

title: Flicker predicts failure: temporal inconsistency as free uncertainty in video
problem: Frame-to-frame prediction flicker in video is treated as a nuisance, but it may be a well-calibrated free uncertainty signal identifying which detections are unreliable without any labels.
hypothesis: Per-object flicker statistics predict per-object error (false positive or misclassification) with useful precision, outperforming raw confidence as an error-flagging signal on video benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Compute flicker features and error labels on cached video predictions of 4 detectors; analysis only.

title: Valid conformal boxes: what is the right nonconformity score for detection
problem: Conformal prediction promises distribution-free coverage for boxes, but detection has structured outputs (matching, suppression) where naive nonconformity scores may badly over- or under-cover.
hypothesis: Coverage validity and interval efficiency vary widely across candidate nonconformity scores (corner residuals, IoU-based, score-normalized), and a matching-aware score achieves target coverage with intervals half the size of naive scores.
cheapest_experiment: Implement 4 nonconformity scores over cached predictions with held-out calibration split; analysis only.

title: Scaling attacks: detection failures induced by downsampling pipelines
problem: Production pipelines downsample images before detection; adversarial and accidental aliasing in the resize step can alter detections, an attack and reliability surface that detection benchmarks never exercise.
hypothesis: Content invisible at full resolution but revealed by specific downsampling kernels can create or suppress detections, and common production resize defaults are more vulnerable than antialiased alternatives by a measurable factor.
cheapest_experiment: Construct scaling-attack images against 2 resize kernels, measure detection deltas across 3 detectors; small optimization plus inference.

title: Threshold drift under mild shift: the silent killer of deployed detectors
problem: Deployments fix a confidence threshold tuned on validation data, but mild distribution shift moves the score distribution so the effective operating point drifts, a failure channel distinct from AP loss and rarely measured.
hypothesis: Under mild shifts that reduce AP by under 2 points, the precision at a fixed threshold can degrade several times more than AP suggests, and score-distribution matching restores most of the loss without retraining.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate fixed-threshold precision vs AP under a battery of mild shifts for 5 detectors, test quantile-matching correction; inference only.

title: Perturb-and-agree: cheap input-perturbation UQ vs deep ensembles
problem: Deep ensembles are the UQ gold standard but cost multiple models; agreement across cheap input perturbations of a single model might recover most of the uncertainty quality at a fraction of the cost.
hypothesis: Detection uncertainty from agreement over K mild input perturbations achieves at least 80 percent of ensemble risk-coverage utility at one-third the compute, uniformly across shift levels.
cheapest_experiment: Compare perturbation-agreement UQ vs a 3-model ensemble on clean and shifted data for 2 architectures; inference-scale compute.

title: Does adversarial pretraining transfer robustness to detection finetunes
problem: Robust backbones are advertised as robustness sources for downstream tasks, but detection finetuning may erase adversarially learned invariances, and nobody has isolated how much survives.
hypothesis: Detection finetunes of adversarially pretrained backbones retain corruption robustness but lose most norm-bounded adversarial robustness, quantifying which invariances survive task transfer.
cheapest_experiment: Finetune robust and standard backbones identically, evaluate both robustness types; two finetunes plus inference.

title: Low-light detection: ISP-aware augmentation vs raw-domain training
problem: Low-light robustness work augments processed sRGB images, but real low-light degradation happens before the ISP; whether raw-domain training buys anything over ISP-aware augmentation is an open, deployment-relevant question.
hypothesis: Training on physically modeled raw-domain noise piped through the target ISP beats equivalent sRGB-space augmentation on real night captures by a margin that justifies the pipeline complexity only below a threshold light level.
cheapest_experiment: Two training runs (raw-modeled vs sRGB augmentation) evaluated on public real night detection sets; two training runs.

title: A cheap failure alarm: predicting detector errors from internal features
problem: Deployments need per-image failure alarms; internal detector features may support a tiny error-predictor head that flags failures more reliably than confidence heuristics, but this has not been benchmarked as a standard component.
hypothesis: A lightweight probe on frozen internal features predicts image-level detection failure (AP below a floor) with a precision-recall profile substantially better than confidence-aggregate baselines, and transfers across mild shifts.
cheapest_experiment: Train the probe on val-split failures of one detector, test under shifts; probe training only.

title: Score-distribution drift as an early-warning system for silent model decay
problem: Deployed detectors decay silently; label-free monitoring from score-distribution drift could provide early warnings, but the lead time between drift signals and actual AP decay is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Distributional drift statistics on detection scores detect AP degradation with useful lead time (drift alarm precedes a 2-point AP drop) across simulated deployment streams.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate deployment streams with gradual shifts, compare drift-alarm timing vs labeled AP trajectories for 3 detectors; inference-scale compute.

title: Gaussian augmentation does not model sensors: shot-noise-matched robustness
problem: Noise robustness is trained with Gaussian noise, but real sensor noise is signal-dependent (shot noise dominated); the mismatch may leave detectors fragile exactly in dark regions where it matters.
hypothesis: Detectors augmented with physically parameterized shot-read noise beat Gaussian-augmented ones on real high-ISO captures, with the advantage concentrated in dark image regions.
cheapest_experiment: Two training runs (Gaussian vs physical noise model) evaluated on real high-ISO test data; two training runs.

title: Calibrated counting: prediction intervals for object counts from detections
problem: Many applications consume object counts derived from detections, but no standard method provides calibrated prediction intervals on counts, and naive per-detection independence assumptions are provably wrong under NMS coupling.
hypothesis: Count intervals built from score-threshold sweeps with conformal calibration achieve nominal coverage where independence-based intervals undercover badly, across density regimes.
cheapest_experiment: Construct both interval types from cached predictions on counting-style datasets, measure empirical coverage; analysis only.

title: Decomposing the syn2real gap: content, appearance, and label convention
problem: The synthetic-to-real detection gap is reported as one number, hiding that it mixes content mismatch (what scenes contain), appearance mismatch (how things look), and label-convention mismatch (how boxes are drawn), each demanding different fixes.
hypothesis: Using controlled renders that vary one factor at a time, the syn2real AP gap decomposes with content mismatch as the largest component for driving scenes, contradicting the appearance-centric focus of current adaptation research.
cheapest_experiment: Render matched scene sets varying content realism vs appearance realism separately in CARLA, train identical detectors, test on real data; a few rendering and training runs.

title: Fidelity return-on-effort curves for simulation axes
problem: Simulation teams invest in geometry, materials, lighting, and sensor modeling without knowing which axis buys the most downstream detection AP per unit of engineering effort.
hypothesis: AP-per-effort curves across fidelity axes are strongly unequal, with sensor modeling (noise, ISP, optics) dominating material realism for detection transfer, enabling rational simulator budgets.
cheapest_experiment: Ablate fidelity axes independently in an open simulator with effort proxies logged, train and test detectors per cell; a bounded grid of renders and short trains.

title: Synthetic data only for the tail: hybrid real-head syn-tail training
problem: Synthetic data is usually mixed indiscriminately with real data, but its value may concentrate entirely in rare classes where real examples are scarce, changing how synthetic pipelines should be targeted.
hypothesis: Restricting synthetic data to tail classes achieves the same tail-AP gains as full-distribution synthetic mixing at a tenth of the rendering budget, with less head-class interference.
cheapest_experiment: Compare full-mix vs tail-only synthetic augmentation at matched rendering budgets on a long-tail benchmark; two or three training runs.

title: Per-class geography sensitivity of AV detection
problem: Cross-geography degradation of driving detectors is reported as aggregate AP, hiding that some classes (signage, vehicles) shift much more than others (pedestrians), which matters for what data to collect where.
hypothesis: Per-class AP drop across geographies is highly unequal and predictable from class-specific appearance variance across regions, enabling targeted data collection that recovers most of the gap at a fraction of full-region labeling cost.
cheapest_experiment: Cross-evaluate public models across geographic splits of existing AV datasets, build the per-class shift table; inference only.

title: Small objects break sim transfer first: size-stratified syn2real analysis
problem: Syn2real studies report pooled AP, but rendering artifacts (aliasing, texture minification) plausibly hit small objects hardest, meaning simulation may be unusable specifically for the small-object regime it is often bought for.
hypothesis: The syn2real AP gap grows monotonically as object size shrinks, and supersampled rendering closes a large share of the small-object gap without any domain adaptation.
cheapest_experiment: Train on standard vs supersampled renders, evaluate size-stratified AP on real data; two renders plus two training runs.

title: Feature-distance domain metrics do not predict AP drop
problem: Domain gap is routinely quantified with feature-space distances (MMD, Frechet), but whether these numbers predict actual detection AP drop across domain pairs is largely assumed.
hypothesis: Across 20 domain pairs, feature-distance metrics explain under half the variance in AP drop, while a cheap proxy task (unsupervised box-statistics divergence) predicts it substantially better.
cheapest_experiment: Assemble 20 source-target pairs from public datasets, compute candidate predictors vs measured AP drops of fixed models; inference and analysis only.

title: Physics-based weather rendering vs GAN translation at matched effort
problem: Two schools produce bad-weather training data (physical rendering vs learned translation), and practitioners lack a controlled comparison on downstream detection rather than image realism scores.
hypothesis: At matched data volume, physics-based weather augmentation beats GAN translation for detection robustness on real weather, because translation introduces label-geometry corruption that outweighs its realism advantage.
cheapest_experiment: Generate both augmentation sets from the same clear-weather corpus, train matched detectors, test on real weather sets; two training runs.

title: Label conventions are a domain: quantifying annotation-style shift
problem: Cross-dataset detection drops are attributed to image distribution shift, but annotation-style differences (box tightness, class granularity, crowd handling) constitute a second, unmeasured domain axis.
hypothesis: A convention-translation layer fitted on a small dual-annotated set (images labeled under both conventions) recovers a large fraction of cross-dataset AP drop without touching the images, proving label style is a major gap component.
cheapest_experiment: Dual-annotate 300 images under two dataset conventions, fit the translation, re-evaluate cross-dataset transfer; small annotation plus analysis.

title: Scaling laws for rendered data: where does synthetic volume saturate
problem: Synthetic data pipelines can generate unbounded volume, but the AP-vs-render-count curve and its saturation point for detection are unpublished, so teams over- or under-render blindly.
hypothesis: Detection AP follows a power law in rendered-image count that saturates at a volume determined by asset diversity, not image count, making asset count the binding constraint.
cheapest_experiment: Train on nested render volumes at 2 asset-diversity levels, fit curves; six short training runs on existing sim stacks.

title: What transfers to exotic sensors: RGB-trained detectors on thermal, event, and fisheye
problem: Practitioners bootstrap exotic-sensor detection from RGB-pretrained models, but which architectural components (backbone layers, necks, heads) carry transferable structure across sensor types is unmapped.
hypothesis: Transfer to thermal and fisheye preserves value mostly in early and mid backbone layers (measurable by layer-wise re-initialization), while event-camera transfer preserves almost nothing, defining sensor-transfer boundaries.
cheapest_experiment: Layer-wise re-init ablations when finetuning one RGB detector onto public thermal, event, and fisheye datasets; a grid of short finetunes.

title: UDA benchmark rankings vs real deployment pairs: external validity check
problem: Unsupervised domain adaptation methods are ranked on a handful of canonical benchmark pairs (sim-to-city, city-to-city); whether those rankings generalize to arbitrary real deployment pairs is the field's unexamined external-validity assumption.
hypothesis: Method rankings on canonical UDA detection benchmarks correlate weakly with rankings on freshly constructed deployment-style pairs, indicating benchmark overfitting of the UDA field.
cheapest_experiment: Run 5 public UDA methods on 5 non-canonical pairs assembled from existing datasets, compare rank orders; a bounded set of adaptation runs.

title: Night is an ISP artifact: disentangling photons from processing
problem: Day-night domain shift conflates photon-level changes with in-camera processing behavior changes (denoising, tone mapping at high gain), and which component breaks detectors determines whether fixes belong in the ISP or the model.
hypothesis: Replaying night raw captures through a day-tuned ISP recovers a substantial share of the night AP drop, showing that a large fraction of the night domain gap is manufactured by processing choices rather than light physics.
cheapest_experiment: Use a raw night dataset, process under two ISP configurations, evaluate fixed detectors; processing plus inference.

title: Asset diversity vs asset count: what actually drives sim transfer
problem: Synthetic pipelines multiply scenes from limited 3D asset libraries, and the marginal value of a new unique asset vs another instantiation of existing assets is unknown, though it dominates content-creation budgets.
hypothesis: At matched render count, 100 unique assets instantiated 100 times each beat 10 assets instantiated 1,000 times by a large AP margin, and the diversity effect saturates predictably, yielding an asset-budget rule.
cheapest_experiment: Render matched sets at 4 diversity levels, train and evaluate matched detectors; four renders plus four short trains.

title: Randomization breadth vs volume: isolating the active ingredient
problem: Domain randomization mixes two variables (how broadly parameters vary and how many samples are drawn), and their separate contributions to detection transfer have not been isolated.
hypothesis: Transfer AP depends primarily on randomization breadth with rapidly diminishing returns to volume at fixed breadth, so small broadly-randomized sets beat large narrow ones at equal render cost.
cheapest_experiment: Cross breadth x volume in a 3x3 render grid with matched detectors; nine short training runs.

title: Can simulators evaluate detectors: real2sim validity for rankings
problem: Evaluating detectors in simulation would be cheap and safe, but whether sim-measured rankings and failure modes match real-world ones (the real2sim eval question) lacks a direct validation study.
hypothesis: Detector rankings measured in a high-fidelity simulator correlate strongly with real-data rankings for aggregate AP but break down for failure-mode-specific metrics (occlusion, night), bounding what simulation can certify.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 8 public detectors on matched sim and real scenes, compare rankings globally and per stratum; inference only.

title: Watching confirmation bias happen: class drift in pseudo-label adaptation
problem: Self-training adaptation is known to reinforce its own errors, but the dynamics (which classes drift, how fast, and what early signals predict collapse) have not been measured longitudinally in detection.
hypothesis: Pseudo-label class distributions drift measurably toward head classes over adaptation rounds, the drift rate predicts final failure, and a simple distribution-anchoring constraint prevents most of it.
cheapest_experiment: Instrument a standard self-training adaptation loop with per-round class-distribution logging on one benchmark pair; a few adaptation runs.

title: How far does amplitude-swap go: the embarrassing FFT baseline for detection UDA
problem: Fourier amplitude swapping is a trivially cheap domain-alignment trick; establishing how much of published UDA gains it captures would recalibrate the field's sense of progress.
hypothesis: FFT amplitude alignment alone captures more than half of the AP gain of published UDA detection methods on standard benchmarks at essentially zero training complexity.
cheapest_experiment: Train source models with amplitude-swapped augmentation on 3 benchmark pairs, compare against published UDA numbers; three short training runs.

title: The HD-to-SD gap: cross-resolution deployment as a neglected domain axis
problem: Models trained on high-resolution benchmark imagery are deployed on low-bitrate CCTV and drone feeds; cross-resolution shift is a distinct, quantifiable domain axis that adaptation research largely skips.
hypothesis: Training-resolution mismatch accounts for a larger AP drop than the appearance-domain mismatch in typical surveillance deployments, and resolution-matched finetuning beats generic UDA methods on such pairs.
cheapest_experiment: Construct HD-train SD-test pairs by controlled degradation of existing datasets, compare resolution-matched finetuning vs one UDA method; a few short runs.

title: Seasonal decay curves: measuring detection model rot in fixed deployments
problem: Fixed-camera deployments experience slow seasonal and infrastructural drift, but the community has no published decay curves quantifying how fast detection quality rots without retraining.
hypothesis: Detection AP in fixed-camera settings decays measurably over months with season as the dominant factor, and a compact set of drift features predicts when retraining is worthwhile.
cheapest_experiment: Use public long-duration camera archives with sparse labeling to estimate quarterly AP of a frozen model; annotation of a few hundred frames per quarter.

title: Synthetic occlusions are too clean: an occlusion-statistics audit of sim datasets
problem: Simulated datasets claim occlusion coverage, but their occlusion statistics (overlap topology, occluder classes, boundary complexity) may diverge from real scenes, silently limiting transfer for the crowded scenes sim is meant to cover.
hypothesis: Popular synthetic driving datasets differ significantly from real counterparts in occlusion statistics, and re-sampling synthetic scenes to match real occlusion statistics improves transfer AP on occluded strata without new assets.
cheapest_experiment: Compute occlusion-statistics divergence between sim and real datasets, re-sample sim training accordingly, retrain once; analysis plus one training run.

title: Do foundation backbones retire detection UDA: a gap-closure audit
problem: Domain adaptation methods were developed for ImageNet-pretrained backbones; if modern foundation backbones already close most of the syn2real gap, the UDA toolbox needs re-justification against this new baseline.
hypothesis: Switching to a modern foundation backbone closes more of the syn2real detection gap than the best published UDA method applied to the old backbone, and stacking UDA on the new backbone adds little.
cheapest_experiment: Four training runs (2 backbones x plain vs one UDA method) on a standard syn2real pair; four training runs.

title: Known objects in unknown places: compositional shift without appearance shift
problem: Domain shift research focuses on appearance, but deployment surprises are often compositional (familiar objects in unfamiliar contexts), and detectors' compositional generalization is unmeasured separately from appearance robustness.
hypothesis: Detectors lose substantial AP on context-swapped renders (correct object appearance, implausible context) even with zero appearance shift, and the loss correlates with the strength of learned context priors per class.
cheapest_experiment: Composite objects into implausible contexts with matched lighting using existing assets, evaluate 5 detectors; compositing plus inference.

title: Sim-trained auto-labelers plus human verification: the cost curve nobody published
problem: A practical syn2real route is to auto-label real data with sim-trained models and pay humans only to verify, but the verification-cost vs final-AP curve that would justify this pipeline is unpublished.
hypothesis: Verification-based labeling reaches 95 percent of full-manual-label AP at under a third of the annotation cost for typical driving scenes, with the ratio predictable from the auto-labeler's precision.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate the pipeline on an already-labeled dataset (verification decisions replayed from GT), sweep verification budgets, train students; analysis plus a few short trains.

title: Renderer fingerprints: does mixing renderers prevent sim-specific overfitting
problem: Models trained on one renderer may latch onto renderer-specific artifacts (antialiasing patterns, tone mapping), and whether multi-renderer blending prevents this overfitting is untested despite being cheap to implement.
hypothesis: Detectors trained on one renderer transfer worse to real data than matched-volume multi-renderer blends, and a renderer-classifier probe on their features confirms fingerprint absorption as the mechanism.
cheapest_experiment: Train on single vs blended renders from 2 open simulators at matched volume, probe features for renderer identity; three training runs plus probes.

title: Depth-sensor simulation gap for RGB-D detection
problem: RGB-D detection research uses simulated depth with idealized noise, but real depth sensors fail in structured ways (edges, dark and specular surfaces), and the transfer cost of the idealization is unquantified.
hypothesis: RGB-D detectors trained on idealized simulated depth lose most of their depth-derived advantage on real sensor data, and injecting a measured sensor-noise model during training recovers the majority of it.
cheapest_experiment: Train with idealized vs measured-noise-model depth on existing RGB-D datasets, evaluate on real captures; two training runs.

title: Does super-resolution help detection or just fool metrics
problem: SR is routinely inserted before small-object detection, but SR models hallucinate plausible texture; the community has not separated genuine information recovery from hallucination that happens to please detectors trained on similar priors.
hypothesis: SR preprocessing improves small-object AP on benchmark data but yields zero or negative gains on a ground-truth-controlled setup (real high-res images downsampled, detection compared against the true high-res content), exposing part of reported SR gains as shared-prior artifacts.
cheapest_experiment: Build a controlled pipeline (true HR, downsample, SR, detect) on COCO and VisDrone, compare against direct low-res detection and true-HR upper bound for 3 SR models x 3 detectors; inference only.

title: Perceptual SR quality and detection utility are anti-correlated in the hallucination regime
problem: SR models are ranked by perceptual metrics (LPIPS, user studies), but downstream detection cares about factual content; the relationship between perceptual rank and detection utility across the fidelity-hallucination spectrum is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Beyond a fidelity threshold, SR models with better perceptual scores produce worse detection truthfulness (more spurious and shifted detections), making perceptual rank a misleading guide for analytics pipelines.
cheapest_experiment: Score 8 public SR models on perceptual metrics and on detection truthfulness in the controlled HR-downsample protocol; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Hallucinated-label noise rates in diffusion-generated detection training data
problem: Diffusion-generated images with auto-derived boxes are entering detection training sets, but the rate at which generation and auto-labeling jointly fabricate wrong labels (phantom objects, wrong classes) is unreported.
hypothesis: Human audit of popular generated-detection-data pipelines finds label fabrication rates far above accepted human annotation error rates, and training contamination at these rates measurably hurts clean-data AP.
cheapest_experiment: Audit 1,000 generated image-label pairs from a public pipeline, then train with controlled contamination doses; small annotation plus a few short trains.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Denoise-then-detect vs noise-robust training: an end-to-end accounting
problem: Pipelines either clean images before detection or train detectors to tolerate noise; the comparison is usually made on image metrics rather than detection outcomes at matched total compute.
hypothesis: Noise-robust detection training dominates denoise-then-detect on real noisy captures at matched inference compute, because denoisers remove small-object evidence along with noise.
cheapest_experiment: Compare both pipelines on real high-ISO data with matched budgets, stratify by object size; one training run plus inference.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Detections that exist only after SR are hallucinations: a consistency flag
problem: When a detection appears in the SR output but has no support in the low-res input, it is likely hallucinated, suggesting a zero-training flag for SR-induced fabrications that analytics pipelines currently lack.
hypothesis: SR-only detections (absent from low-res inference at any threshold) are dominated by hallucinations, verified against true HR content, with precision above 80 percent as a fabrication detector.
cheapest_experiment: In the controlled HR-downsample protocol, compute SR-only detections and verify against true HR labels; analysis only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Restoration erases small objects: measuring the object-destruction rate
problem: Denoisers and deblurrers are optimized for aggregate image quality and may treat small real objects as noise to remove, a catastrophic failure for downstream detection that image metrics cannot see.
hypothesis: State-of-the-art restoration models measurably erase or degrade a nonzero fraction of true small objects (detectable before, undetectable after restoration against GT), and the erasure rate grows as object size approaches the noise scale.
cheapest_experiment: Run restoration on degraded images with known GT, measure per-size detectability before vs after for 4 restoration models; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Generative vs physically-consistent deblurring for video analytics truthfulness
problem: Generative deblurring produces sharp, plausible frames that may relocate or re-render moving objects, and video analytics consumes these frames as evidence without any truthfulness measurement.
hypothesis: Generative deblurrers shift object positions and alter object identity at rates significantly above physically-constrained deblurring, measurable as detection-box displacement against sharp GT frames.
cheapest_experiment: Use datasets with paired blurred-sharp frames (GoPro-style), compare box displacement and identity flips after each deblurring type; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: The bitrate threshold below which artifact removal helps detection
problem: Compression-artifact removal is applied uniformly before analytics, but it plausibly helps only below some bitrate while wasting compute or hurting above it; the threshold has never been mapped.
hypothesis: Artifact-removal preprocessing improves detection AP only below a codec-specific bitrate threshold, above which it is neutral or harmful, and the threshold is stable across content types.
cheapest_experiment: Sweep bitrate x artifact-removal on-off, evaluate 3 detectors; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Does insertion realism matter: diffusion object insertion vs naive paste for detection training
problem: Diffusion inpainting can insert objects photorealistically for augmentation, at high compute cost; whether realism (lighting, shadows, harmonization) actually buys AP over naive copy-paste is the economic question nobody has answered cleanly.
hypothesis: Detection gains from object-insertion augmentation are insensitive to insertion realism: naive paste matches diffusion-harmonized insertion at equal instance counts, implying the gains are label-distribution effects.
cheapest_experiment: Three matched training runs (no insertion, naive paste, diffusion insertion) at fixed inserted-instance counts; three training runs.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Diversity beats fidelity for generative tail-class data
problem: Generative augmentation for rare classes can spend compute on fidelity (better samples) or diversity (more varied samples), and downstream detection AP should adjudicate this trade-off, not image metrics.
hypothesis: At matched sample count, higher-diversity lower-fidelity generation (higher guidance-scale variance, prompt variety) beats high-fidelity narrow generation for tail-class AP, because coverage matters more than realism for rare classes.
cheapest_experiment: Generate two matched tail-class sets along the fidelity-diversity axis, train matched detectors on LVIS-tail; two training runs plus generation.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: SR as test-time compute: does it ever beat native high-resolution inference
problem: SR-then-detect spends compute to upsample before detection, but the same compute could run the detector at higher input resolution directly; the comparison at matched FLOPs is the decision practitioners actually face.
hypothesis: At matched total inference FLOPs, native high-resolution detection dominates SR-then-detect across SR architectures, leaving no compute regime where SR preprocessing is the rational choice.
cheapest_experiment: FLOP-matched grid of SR-plus-detector vs upscaled-input detector on VisDrone; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Task-loss SR overfits its detector: transferability of detection-aware SR
problem: SR models trained with detection-task losses report downstream gains, but if those gains are specific to the detector used in training, the approach fails the modularity requirement of real pipelines.
hypothesis: Detection-aware SR gains collapse when the downstream detector is swapped (different family or training data), revealing the SR model learned detector-specific score inflation rather than information recovery.
cheapest_experiment: Train one detection-aware SR model against detector A, evaluate downstream with detectors B, C, D; one SR training run plus inference.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Identity fabrication in face and plate SR: measuring evidentiary harm
problem: SR applied to faces and license plates fabricates identity-bearing detail, and downstream recognition systems consume it; the fabrication rate as measured by verification models is a safety-critical unknown.
hypothesis: SR of genuinely low-information face and plate crops produces outputs that verification models match to wrong identities at rates far above the low-res baseline, quantifying SR as an evidence-corruption channel.
cheapest_experiment: Downsample identity-labeled face/plate data below the information threshold, SR it, run verification against galleries; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Feature-space SR vs pixel-space SR: where is the small-object bottleneck
problem: If the information bottleneck for small objects lies in early feature extraction, upsampling backbone features should match pixel SR at far lower cost; the comparison localizes where resolution actually matters.
hypothesis: Learned feature upsampling inside the detector matches pixel-space SR preprocessing on small-object AP at a fraction of the FLOPs, showing the pixel-space detour is wasteful.
cheapest_experiment: Compare pixel-SR preprocessing vs feature-upsampling head modifications at matched accuracy targets; two training runs plus inference.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Training on generated images plants fingerprints: bias transfer from diffusion data to detectors
problem: As generated images enter detection training corpora, detectors may absorb generator-specific artifacts and content biases, changing behavior on real data in ways nobody is monitoring.
hypothesis: Detectors trained with a substantial generated-data fraction show measurable behavioral shifts on real data (class-prior drift toward generator biases, texture-sensitivity changes), detectable even when clean AP is unchanged.
cheapest_experiment: Train matched detectors at 0, 25, and 50 percent generated-data fractions, compare behavioral fingerprints on real probes; three training runs.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Synthetic degradations mislead restoration research: detection utility on real degradations
problem: Restoration models are benchmarked on synthetic degradations; if their detection-utility ranking reverses on real degraded captures, the restoration leaderboard misleads everyone building analytics pipelines.
hypothesis: The ranking of restoration models by downstream detection AP on real degraded data disagrees substantially with their ranking on standard synthetic-degradation benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 6 restoration models by downstream detection on real low-quality datasets vs synthetic benchmarks; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Text-to-image data vs 3D rendering for detection pretraining at matched cost
problem: Two synthetic-data routes compete (prompted diffusion generation vs 3D rendering with exact labels), differing in label fidelity and content diversity; a cost-matched downstream comparison for detection does not exist.
hypothesis: At matched dollar cost, 3D-rendered data with exact geometry labels beats diffusion-generated data with derived labels for detection pretraining, because label noise dominates content diversity in the current regime.
cheapest_experiment: Produce cost-matched corpora via both routes for one domain, pretrain and finetune matched detectors; two data pipelines plus two training runs.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Objects drift under img2img augmentation: quantifying geometric label corruption
problem: Img2img diffusion augmentation subtly moves and reshapes objects, corrupting box labels in ways augmented-training pipelines silently absorb; the drift statistics have not been published.
hypothesis: Standard img2img augmentation strengths displace object boundaries by amounts that exceed annotation-noise levels, and training with drift-corrected boxes (re-derived from the augmented image) recovers measurable AP.
