cheapest_experiment: Measure box displacement distributions across augmentation strengths using segmentation-model re-localization, then compare training with original vs corrected boxes; analysis plus two short trains.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Annotation misalignment when training on SR images with original boxes
problem: Pipelines that upsample archival low-res datasets with SR reuse the original box annotations, but SR subtly shifts content, creating a systematic train-time label misalignment nobody has quantified.
hypothesis: Training on SR-upsampled images with original-resolution boxes introduces localization bias measurable at test time, and re-deriving boxes on the SR output eliminates it.
cheapest_experiment: Train matched detectors on SR data with original vs re-derived boxes, compare localization error profiles; two short training runs.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Temporal consistency beats per-frame quality: video SR for video detection
problem: Video SR models are ranked by per-frame quality, but downstream video detection may care more about temporal consistency of the reconstruction than about any single frame's fidelity.
hypothesis: Across video SR models, downstream video-detection quality correlates more strongly with temporal-consistency measures than with per-frame reconstruction metrics, reversing some model rankings.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 5 video SR models by both metric families and by downstream detection on low-res video benchmarks; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Learned codecs and detection: is machine-oriented compression actually better for machines
problem: Learned compression claims machine-task advantages over classical codecs, but detection evaluations are scattered and rarely bitrate-matched with strong classical baselines properly tuned for analytics.
hypothesis: At matched bitrates with analytics-tuned classical codec settings, learned codecs offer no consistent detection AP advantage in the bitrate range used by real deployments.
cheapest_experiment: Rate-distortion-detection curves for 2 learned codecs vs tuned H.265/JPEG on COCO and a surveillance dataset; inference only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Detection-grounded evaluation of generative models: counting and layout fidelity
problem: FID-style metrics ignore whether generated scenes have coherent object structure; detectors could measure object-count, co-occurrence, and layout fidelity, giving generative evaluation a dense-prediction foundation.
hypothesis: A detection-grounded scene-structure score separates generative models that FID ranks as equivalent, and correlates better with human judgments of scene coherence than FID does.
cheapest_experiment: Compute detection-based structure statistics on samples from 6 generative models, compare with FID and a small human study; inference plus small study.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Which way does SR lie: asymmetry of hallucinated additions vs deletions
problem: SR errors are treated as symmetric noise, but generative SR may systematically add plausible objects rather than remove real ones (or vice versa), and the error direction determines the harm profile for surveillance vs inspection uses.
hypothesis: Generative SR exhibits a strong asymmetry toward object addition (phantom small objects) over deletion, and the asymmetry grows with the generative prior strength of the SR model.
cheapest_experiment: In the controlled HR-downsample protocol, classify SR-induced detection errors into additions and deletions across 5 SR models; analysis only.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Enhancement for humans vs enhancement for detectors: two different optima
problem: Low-light enhancement is tuned for human-viewed image quality, and deployments reuse the same enhancement for machine analytics, assuming one optimum serves both; the divergence between the two optima is unmeasured.
hypothesis: The enhancement parameter settings maximizing human-rated quality differ systematically from those maximizing detection AP on the same images, and the human-optimal setting sacrifices multiple AP points relative to the machine-optimal one.
cheapest_experiment: Sweep enhancement parameters on real night data, measure detection AP curves and collect small-scale human ratings; inference plus small study.

cluster: SR, restoration, generation, diffusion tied to dense prediction
title: Recapture and re-enhancement loops: pipeline-artifact distributions detectors never trained on
problem: Real-world images increasingly pass through enhancement, recompression, and screen-recapture loops, creating compound artifact distributions absent from training data, and detector behavior on them is unknown despite their prevalence in user-generated content.
hypothesis: Detection AP on multi-stage-processed images (enhance, compress, recapture) drops substantially more than the sum of single-stage drops predicts, revealing compounding nonlinearity that single-corruption benchmarks miss.
cheapest_experiment: Build a processing-chain corruption suite, evaluate 5 detectors on single vs compound chains; inference only.

title: Photographer framing bias: the decentered test set
problem: Detection datasets inherit photographer composition habits (objects centered, canonical scale and viewpoint), so benchmark AP may overstate performance on machine-captured imagery (fixed cameras, robots) where framing is arbitrary.
hypothesis: Detectors lose substantial AP on a test set re-composed to uniform object position and scale distributions (via crops of wider captures), and the loss exceeds what position statistics alone predict, indicating deeper framing-correlated features.
cheapest_experiment: Construct decentered evaluations by cropping panoramic or wide-angle datasets to controlled framing distributions, evaluate 6 detectors; data wrangling plus inference.

title: Geographic performance audit with a purpose-built geo-stratified test set
problem: Detection models are deployed globally but evaluated on geographically skewed data; per-region AP differences for common classes are anecdotal rather than measured under controlled protocols.
hypothesis: Per-region AP on a geo-stratified test set varies by margins comparable to several years of benchmark progress, and the variation correlates with training-data geographic density per class.
cheapest_experiment: Annotate a modest geo-stratified sample from openly licensed global street imagery under one protocol, evaluate public detectors; annotation budget dominated.

title: Class granularity is a hidden progress knob
problem: Benchmarks decide arbitrarily which concepts get their own class (many dog breeds vs one plant class), and this granularity choice shapes measured progress in ways never quantified.
hypothesis: Re-partitioning benchmark taxonomies at coarser or finer granularity changes both absolute AP and method rankings, with fine-grained partitions penalizing exactly the models that lead current leaderboards.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score cached predictions under merged and split taxonomies built from WordNet on COCO and LVIS; re-analysis only.

title: Do LVIS-tuned long-tail methods survive contact with real deployment tails
problem: Long-tail detection methods are developed against LVIS's specific tail structure; natural deployment tails (retail catalogs, wildlife cameras) have different shape and semantics, and transfer is assumed rather than measured.
hypothesis: Method rankings on LVIS tail metrics correlate weakly with rankings on naturally long-tailed deployment datasets, exposing LVIS overfitting in the long-tail literature.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 5 published long-tail methods on 3 naturally long-tailed public datasets, compare rank orders with LVIS; finetuning plus inference.

title: Head-class sacrifice accounting: is total utility actually improved by long-tail methods
problem: Long-tail methods trade head-class AP for tail-class AP, and whether the trade improves total deployment utility depends on instance frequencies that macro metrics deliberately ignore.
hypothesis: Under instance-frequency-weighted utility (each detection event weighted by its deployment frequency), most published long-tail methods reduce total utility relative to the plain baseline.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score cached predictions of long-tail methods under frequency-weighted utilities across plausible deployment priors; re-analysis only.

title: Small and rare are confounded: disentangling size from frequency in long-tail claims
problem: In natural datasets, rare classes are disproportionately small objects, so long-tail improvements may actually be small-object improvements in disguise, misdirecting the field's causal story.
hypothesis: After stratifying by object size, a large fraction of reported tail-AP gains from representative long-tail methods disappears, showing the methods act through the size channel rather than the frequency channel.
cheapest_experiment: Size-stratified re-analysis of cached predictions from 4 long-tail methods on LVIS; re-analysis only.

title: Watermarks and stock-photo artifacts as shortcut features in web-scraped detection data
problem: Web-scraped detection corpora contain watermarks, borders, and stock-photo staging correlated with specific classes, providing shortcut features whose contribution to benchmark AP is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Ablating watermark-and-border artifacts at test time (inpainting them away) reduces AP for web-trained detectors on affected classes measurably more than for detectors trained on curated data.
cheapest_experiment: Detect and inpaint watermark artifacts on affected test images, compare AP deltas across differently-trained models; analysis plus inference.

title: Person-detection fairness with proper uncertainty: a benchmark that supports conclusions
problem: Person-detection fairness studies report subgroup miss-rate gaps without adequate statistical treatment, and dataset sizes often cannot support the published conclusions in either direction.
hypothesis: With subgroup-stratified confidence intervals on adequately powered data, some widely-cited subgroup gaps in person detection are confirmed while others are statistically unsupportable at current benchmark sizes, and the field's evidentiary base needs rebuilding.
cheapest_experiment: Power analysis of existing fairness benchmarks, then targeted annotation to reach adequacy on the underpowered strata, re-evaluate standard detectors; annotation-bounded.

title: What counts as an object: annotator salience bias in dataset construction
problem: Annotators label what draws attention, so datasets encode a salience-filtered definition of objecthood; the unlabeled-but-arguably-object background content shapes both training and the false-positive accounting of every benchmark.
hypothesis: A dense re-annotation pass (label everything nameable) on a benchmark subset finds a large population of unlabeled objects concentrated in low-salience strata, and standard detectors' 'false positives' overlap heavily with this population.
cheapest_experiment: Exhaustively annotate 200 images, quantify the unlabeled-object population, re-score detector false positives against it; annotation-bounded.

title: Benchmark monoculture: does COCO ranking predict ranking anywhere else
problem: Method development optimizes for COCO, assuming its rankings generalize; the cross-benchmark rank correlation that would validate this assumption has not been published systematically for modern methods.
hypothesis: The rank correlation of 15 modern detectors between COCO and each of 10 diverse detection datasets is high for aggregate AP but collapses for size-, density-, and domain-specific strata, meaning COCO ranking is only trustworthy for aggregate claims.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate 15 public checkpoints across 10 public datasets, compute stratified rank correlations; inference only, highly reusable artifact.

title: Which tail is the tail: image, instance, and pixel frequency define different problems
problem: Long-tail research defines rarity by instance count, but classes can be rare in images, instances, or pixels with different practical consequences, and methods may help one tail while hurting another.
hypothesis: The three rarity definitions produce materially different class orderings on standard datasets, and published long-tail methods improve the instance-count tail while leaving the pixel-count tail (small rare objects) unimproved.
cheapest_experiment: Compute the three tail orderings on LVIS, re-analyze cached long-tail-method predictions per ordering; re-analysis only.

title: Repeat-factor sampling hyperparameters as test-distribution leakage
problem: Long-tail sampling schemes have hyperparameters commonly tuned against the benchmark's test-frequency profile, a subtle leakage channel that inflates the apparent generality of long-tail recipes.
hypothesis: Repeat-factor-style hyperparameters tuned on LVIS transfer poorly to datasets with different tail shapes, and the transferred configurations underperform simple uniform sampling on some of them.
cheapest_experiment: Sweep sampling hyperparameters on LVIS, apply the best to 3 different-tail datasets vs locally-tuned and uniform baselines; several short trains.

title: Stereotyped contexts imprison tail classes: context-swap evaluation for rarity
problem: Rare classes appear in few, stereotyped contexts in training data, so models may only detect them there, but tail evaluation never separates context-typical from context-atypical instances.
hypothesis: Tail-class AP on context-atypical instances (measured via context-swapped composites and rare-context real examples) is a small fraction of context-typical AP, and the gap is larger for tail than head classes at matched instance counts.
cheapest_experiment: Composite tail-class instances into atypical contexts, plus mine rare-context real examples, evaluate 4 detectors; compositing plus inference.

title: Duplicate concentration in the tail inflates rare-class metrics
problem: Web-collected datasets contain near-duplicates that concentrate in rare classes (few source images, many crops), potentially inflating tail metrics through effective train-test leakage within the tail.
hypothesis: Deduplicating tail-class instances across train and test reduces measured tail AP substantially more than head AP, shrinking published long-tail progress.
cheapest_experiment: Run embedding-based duplicate detection per class on LVIS, re-score with duplicates removed; analysis only.

title: Miss-rate parity across density and demographics for crowd person detection
problem: Person detectors in crowds are used for safety decisions, but miss-rate parity across crowd density levels and demographic subgroups jointly has never been benchmarked, though density and demographics interact (who stands where in crowds).
hypothesis: Detector miss rates show a density-demographic interaction (subgroup gaps grow with density), invisible to marginal audits of either factor alone.
cheapest_experiment: Annotate demographics on an existing dense-crowd benchmark subset, evaluate miss rates in the density-by-subgroup grid for 3 detectors; annotation plus inference.

title: Same word, different concept: cross-dataset taxonomy misalignment as measurable noise
problem: Cross-dataset training and evaluation assume class names align semantically, but categories like truck, table, or bag cover different visual concepts per dataset, injecting structured noise into every multi-dataset effort.
hypothesis: For a set of shared class names across 4 datasets, models trained on one dataset misclassify a measurable fraction of another dataset's instances of the same-named class, and the confusion structure matches documented definition differences rather than visual difficulty.
cheapest_experiment: Cross-evaluate per-class confusion of single-dataset models across shared names, adjudicate a sample of confusions manually; inference plus small annotation.

title: Benchmarks age: temporal decay of detection AP on contemporary imagery
problem: Object appearance drifts over years (vehicles, phones, fashion, signage), so models and benchmarks frozen in time may overstate current-world performance, but the decay rate has never been measured for detection.
hypothesis: Detectors trained on decade-old datasets lose AP monotonically on year-stratified contemporary imagery, with class-dependent decay rates largest for design-driven artifacts (phones, cars) and near zero for natural kinds (animals).
cheapest_experiment: Assemble year-stamped test sets from openly licensed imagery, annotate a modest sample per year bucket, evaluate frozen models; annotation-bounded.

title: Tail classes ride on head-class contexts: co-occurrence dependency surgery
problem: Tail-class detections may depend on co-occurring head-class objects as contextual anchors, making tail performance fragile to context changes in ways aggregate tail metrics cannot reveal.
hypothesis: Removing (inpainting) co-occurring head-class objects from scenes reduces tail-class recall substantially more than removing matched background regions, quantifying contextual dependency of the tail.
cheapest_experiment: Inpaint head-class anchors from 500 tail-class scenes, measure tail recall change across 3 detectors; inpainting plus inference.

title: CLIP-filtered data inherits CLIP blind spots: curation bias propagation
problem: Modern detection corpora are curated with CLIP-based filtering, so concepts CLIP represents poorly get systematically excluded, propagating one model's blind spots into all downstream datasets and models.
hypothesis: Classes with weak CLIP zero-shot recognition are underrepresented in CLIP-filtered corpora relative to unfiltered crawls, and detectors trained on filtered corpora show correlated per-class weaknesses, tracing a measurable bias-inheritance chain.
cheapest_experiment: Compare per-class frequencies between filtered and unfiltered crawl samples, correlate with CLIP zero-shot scores and with downstream per-class AP; counting plus inference.

title: Consent and licensing constraints shape dataset content: an absence audit
problem: License-conscious datasets exclude imagery from contexts where consent is hard (homes, hospitals, schools), creating systematic domain absences whose downstream detection consequences are unmeasured.
hypothesis: Detectors trained on license-clean corpora underperform specifically on the absent domains relative to web-trained counterparts at matched aggregate AP, quantifying the cost of ethically-constrained data along domain axes rather than aggregate numbers.
cheapest_experiment: Compare per-domain AP of license-clean vs web-trained public models on domain-stratified evaluations; inference only.

title: Instance-weighted AP lets dense images dominate: the averaging-axis audit
problem: Standard AP pools all instances, so a few dense images dominate the metric, while per-image averaging would weight scenes equally; the choice is consequential and undocumented in most papers.
hypothesis: Switching between instance-pooled and image-averaged AP changes method rankings on dense-scene datasets, and the methods advantaged by instance pooling are systematically those tuned on dense benchmarks.
cheapest_experiment: Re-score cached predictions under both averaging conventions on CrowdHuman and VisDrone; re-analysis only.

title: Benchmarks oversample interesting images: difficulty-distribution mismatch with deployment
problem: Dataset builders select varied, object-rich images, while deployment streams are dominated by boring frames; this difficulty mismatch biases both absolute numbers and method rankings in unknown directions.
hypothesis: Reweighting benchmark evaluation to deployment-like difficulty distributions (mostly sparse frames) changes false-positive-oriented rankings substantially, because methods differ most on empty and near-empty scenes.
cheapest_experiment: Estimate difficulty distributions from public deployment-style streams, reweight benchmark evaluation of 6 detectors accordingly; re-analysis plus light inference.

title: Generative tail augmentation imports generator stereotypes into rare classes
problem: Teams patch tail classes with generated images, but generators render rare concepts in stereotyped ways, potentially narrowing the very distribution the augmentation was meant to broaden.
hypothesis: Tail classes augmented with generated data improve on generator-typical renditions while stagnating or regressing on real atypical instances, measurable by splitting tail test sets along typicality.
cheapest_experiment: Train with and without generative tail augmentation, evaluate on typicality-split tail test sets; two training runs plus a typicality annotation pass.

title: Occlusion and truncation flags are class-biased: an annotation-quality audit
problem: Robustness research relies on occlusion/truncation flags, but flag quality likely varies by class and annotator batch, contaminating every occlusion-stratified conclusion downstream.
hypothesis: Re-adjudicating occlusion flags on a stratified sample reveals class-dependent flag error rates large enough to change occlusion-stratified AP comparisons between detectors.
cheapest_experiment: Re-adjudicate flags on 1,000 instances across classes, quantify error structure, propagate corrections into occlusion-stratified evaluation; small annotation budget.

title: Person subcategory predictions key on clothing and scene, not people
problem: Detectors that emit person subcategories (worker, rider, pedestrian) may rely on clothing and background correlations rather than person-intrinsic evidence, which is a fairness and reliability hazard in safety systems.
hypothesis: Counterfactual edits of clothing and background (segmentation-guided recoloring, context swaps) flip person-subcategory predictions at rates far above the same edits' effect on the base person class, exposing spurious feature dependence.
cheapest_experiment: Apply targeted counterfactual edits to 500 instances, measure subcategory flip rates across 3 models; editing plus inference.

title: The tail-progress illusion: are AP-rare gains concentrated in a few easy classes
problem: Aggregate tail-AP improvements can be driven by a handful of tail classes that are visually easy, while the hard tail stays at zero, but per-class delta distributions are almost never published.
hypothesis: For most published long-tail methods, the majority of AP-rare improvement comes from under a quarter of tail classes, and the median tail class improves negligibly, revising the field's progress narrative.
cheapest_experiment: Compute per-class delta distributions from cached predictions of 5 long-tail methods vs baselines on LVIS; re-analysis only.

title: Tracing one bias end-to-end: from pretraining statistics to detection errors
problem: Bias-inheritance claims (pretraining bias causes downstream detection bias) are plausible but have never been traced quantitatively through the full chain for a single concrete bias.
hypothesis: For a chosen bias axis (indoor vs outdoor context for a class set), pretraining-corpus statistics predict feature-space bias, which predicts detection error asymmetry after finetuning, with each link individually measurable and the chain jointly accounting for most of the final asymmetry.
cheapest_experiment: Instrument all three stages for 2 backbones on one bias axis using public corpora statistics, probes, and stratified detection evaluation; probes plus inference.

title: Standardized budgets for long-tail comparisons: a re-benchmark
problem: Long-tail methods differ in effective epochs over tail instances, extra passes, and memory banks, so published comparisons conflate method merit with hidden budget differences.
hypothesis: Under strictly matched effective-sample budgets per class, the spread between published long-tail methods on LVIS shrinks by more than half, and the surviving ranking differs from the published one.
cheapest_experiment: Re-train 4 methods under a shared budget-accounting harness with 2 seeds; eight training runs.

title: Open-vocab rarity should be measured against pretraining exposure, not dataset counts
problem: Open-vocab methods are credited for rare-class performance where rarity is defined by target-dataset counts, but the models' actual exposure comes from web pretraining, making dataset-defined rarity a misleading axis.
hypothesis: Re-defining class rarity by estimated pretraining exposure reorders the rare-class leaderboard of open-vocab detectors and reveals that exposure-rare classes see little of the claimed open-vocab advantage.
cheapest_experiment: Estimate exposure from public caption corpora, re-stratify existing LVIS evaluations by exposure; counting plus re-analysis.

title: Dataset dignity for stuff classes: what detection loses by ignoring the uncountable
problem: Detection taxonomies exclude stuff (road, grass, water) by design, yet many deployment queries concern stuff-object interactions (person on road), and the cost of the thing-only worldview has not been quantified.
hypothesis: For interaction-style queries, pipelines built on thing-only detectors fail at rates far above pipelines with joint thing-stuff representations at matched compute, quantifying the structural cost of the detection taxonomy choice.
cheapest_experiment: Build 200 interaction queries over existing panoptic datasets, compare detector-only vs panoptic pipelines; inference plus query evaluation.

title: Compute-normalized detection leaderboards: AP as a function of training FLOPs
problem: Detection papers compare endpoint AP while training budgets differ by orders of magnitude, so the literature cannot distinguish methodological progress from compute growth.
hypothesis: When a historical sequence of detection methods is re-trained along matched FLOP budgets, a large fraction of claimed method-over-method gains disappears at equal compute, and the AP-vs-FLOPs frontier moves far less than leaderboards suggest.
cheapest_experiment: Re-train 8 representative methods at 3 matched budget points each with one seed, plot frontiers; a bounded grid of training runs, expensive but foundational.

title: The same method across codebases: framework variance vs claimed deltas
problem: Identical methods produce different AP across mmdetection, detectron2, and YOLO-family codebases, but this framework variance has never been quantified against the size of typical published improvements.
hypothesis: Cross-framework AP variance of the same nominal method exceeds one point for common detectors, overlapping the magnitude of many published method deltas, meaning framework choice is a confound of record.
cheapest_experiment: Train 3 canonical detectors in 3 frameworks under nominally identical configs, 2 seeds each; eighteen short runs.

title: Stale baselines: how much of reported progress is baseline decay
problem: Papers copy baseline numbers from prior work rather than re-running them with modern recipes, so improvements may reflect baseline staleness rather than method merit, an effect size the field has not measured.
hypothesis: Re-running the baselines of 20 recent detection papers with current recipes erases or reverses the claimed improvement in a substantial fraction of cases.
cheapest_experiment: Sample 20 papers with public code, re-train their baselines under the papers' own tuning budgets applied honestly; a bounded set of training runs.

title: How many seeds does detection research need: an empirical power standard
problem: Seed-count conventions in detection are arbitrary because the variance structure of common tasks and recipes is unpublished, so the field cannot say when one seed suffices and when five are needed.
hypothesis: Seed variance varies by an order of magnitude across task regimes (dataset size, schedule length, method family), yielding a practical lookup rule that makes many single-seed papers formally underpowered.
cheapest_experiment: Run 10-seed replicates across a 2x2x2 grid of regimes with small models, publish variance components and the derived seed-count table; many short runs.

title: Shadow tuning: how tuning-budget asymmetry manufactures SOTA
problem: Papers tune their method extensively while baselines get default configs, an asymmetry whose typical effect size on detection benchmarks has never been isolated experimentally.
hypothesis: Granting the baseline the same hyperparameter search budget as the proposed method closes most of the reported gap in a majority of reproducible recent detection papers.
cheapest_experiment: For 6 papers with released code, spend the paper's stated tuning budget on the baseline instead; a bounded tuning-run grid.

title: A decade of adaptive overfitting on test-dev: leaderboard forensics
problem: Repeated evaluations against the same COCO test-dev split should produce community-level adaptive overfitting, detectable through statistical forensics on submission histories, but no one has run the analysis for detection.
hypothesis: Leaderboard submission statistics show the signature of adaptive overfitting (val-test gap growth over time and regression-to-mean of top entries on fresh data), quantifiable without new annotation using existing val-test paired reports.
cheapest_experiment: Assemble published val and test-dev pairs across years, analyze gap dynamics; literature data collection plus statistics.

title: Do published ablations replicate: sign-flip rates under reseeding
problem: Ablation tables are the evidentiary core of method papers yet are usually single-seed; the fraction of ablation conclusions that flip sign under reseeding is an unknown, measurable quantity.
hypothesis: Re-running the ablation tables of representative detection papers with 3 seeds flips the sign of a nontrivial fraction of ablation rows, undermining component-level conclusions across the literature.
cheapest_experiment: Reproduce 5 ablation tables (roughly 30 rows) with 3 seeds each using released code; many short runs, bounded scope.

title: CUDA and cuDNN versions as silent result modifiers
problem: Numerical differences across GPU library versions can shift detection results, but the field lacks a measurement of how much environment versioning alone moves AP relative to claimed effects.
hypothesis: Training the same detection config across 3 CUDA/cuDNN stacks produces AP differences beyond within-stack seed noise for at least some standard recipes, establishing environment version as a reportable variable.
cheapest_experiment: Train one recipe x 3 stacks x 3 seeds in containers; nine short runs.

title: PIL vs OpenCV: preprocessing divergence as an unreported hyperparameter
problem: Image decoding and resizing differ subtly across libraries (color conversion, antialiasing), and mixed train-test preprocessing may shift results by amounts that matter, but the effect has not been isolated for detection.
hypothesis: Train-test preprocessing library mismatch shifts COCO AP measurably (with AP-small most affected), and papers that do not report the preprocessing stack are irreproducible at the precision they claim.
cheapest_experiment: Evaluate fixed checkpoints under crossed decode-resize stacks, then finetune under matched vs mismatched stacks; mostly inference plus two short runs.

title: Determinism audit of popular detection repos
problem: Fixed seeds do not guarantee determinism (data-loading order, atomics, nondeterministic kernels), and the actual reproducibility level of popular detection codebases is undocumented.
hypothesis: A majority of popular detection repos produce different final AP across identical-seed runs, with variance concentrated in data-pipeline nondeterminism rather than kernel nondeterminism, identifiable by controlled toggling.
cheapest_experiment: Run identical-seed replicates in 5 repos with instrumentation isolating nondeterminism sources; several short runs per repo.

title: A reporting-practices census with teeth: re-experiments on the worst gaps
problem: Meta-claims about poor reporting in detection papers are anecdotal; a systematic census tied to targeted re-experiments would turn the complaint into measured science with actionable standards.
hypothesis: Coding 300 recent detection papers reveals that key reproducibility fields (variance, tuning budget, preprocessing stack, compute) are each reported in under a third of papers, and re-experiments show unreported fields correlate with larger reproduction gaps.
cheapest_experiment: Structured coding of 300 papers plus reproduction of 15 with full instrumentation; reading effort plus bounded compute.

title: Ten detection tricks under matched compute: which survive
problem: Widely-adopted training tricks (EMA, mosaic, multi-scale, longer schedules, strong jitter) were validated in different eras and codebases; a single matched-compute revisit would establish which still pay their way.
hypothesis: Under one modern recipe with matched compute accounting, at least a third of canonical detection tricks contribute nothing beyond seed noise, and one or more actively hurt.
cheapest_experiment: Factorial-lite design (each trick toggled from a strong base recipe, 2 seeds) on one mid-size detector; roughly 20 short runs.

title: Latency claims do not replicate: a standardized detection inference benchmark
problem: Published detection latency numbers mix batch sizes, precisions, hardware, and warmup conventions, making cross-paper speed claims incomparable in ways that mislead deployment choices.
hypothesis: Re-measuring 15 detectors under one standardized protocol changes latency-based rankings substantially from published claims, and the discrepancy correlates with measurement-convention choices rather than hardware.
cheapest_experiment: One benchmarking harness, 15 public models, 3 hardware targets; pure measurement.

title: Checkpoint selection by test performance: prevalence and inflation size
problem: Selecting the best checkpoint using test-set metrics is a known but unquantified practice in detection research; its typical inflation size would tell reviewers how much to discount unclear papers.
hypothesis: Best-of-trajectory test selection inflates COCO AP by a measurable margin over last-checkpoint or val-selected reporting, and the inflation grows with evaluation frequency, providing a correction table for meta-analyses.
cheapest_experiment: Instrument several standard training runs with dense checkpointing, compare reporting policies across seeds; a few training runs.

title: Gradient accumulation is not large-batch training: the BN discrepancy audit
problem: Papers treat gradient accumulation as equivalent to large-batch training, but batch statistics differ, and the size of the resulting discrepancy in detection results is unmeasured folklore in both directions.
hypothesis: Accumulation-vs-true-batch discrepancies in final AP exceed seed noise for BN-bearing detectors and vanish for normalization-free variants, cleanly attributing the effect to batch statistics.
cheapest_experiment: Four training runs (accumulated vs true batch, BN vs GN) with 2 seeds; eight short runs.

title: ImageNet init is not one thing: pretrained-weight provenance effects
problem: Papers write ImageNet-pretrained as if it were a single object, but zoo weights differ across versions and recipes, and downstream detection deltas attributed to methods may ride on provenance differences.
hypothesis: Swapping among commonly-used ImageNet checkpoint provenances for the same architecture shifts downstream detection AP by amounts overlapping published method deltas.
cheapest_experiment: Finetune one detector from 5 different same-architecture pretrained checkpoints, 2 seeds; ten short runs.

title: How much does val reuse cost: adaptive overfitting to validation sets
problem: Researchers evaluate on val hundreds of times during development, and the resulting val-specific adaptation inflates val-based conclusions by an amount never measured in detection workflows.
hypothesis: A simulated development process (hyperparameter search guided by val) produces models whose val-test gap grows with the number of adaptive queries, quantifying a per-query overfitting tax for detection.
cheapest_experiment: Run scripted adaptive searches of increasing query counts on split-in-half validation data; a grid of short runs plus analysis.

title: Silent benchmark mutations: a hash-audit of public dataset artifacts
problem: Benchmark annotation files and images change quietly over time (fixes, re-hosting, format migrations), and results across years may be computed against different ground truths without anyone tracking it.
hypothesis: A provenance audit finds multiple materially different versions of widely-used detection benchmark files in circulation, and scoring one model against the variants produces AP differences comparable to published improvements.
cheapest_experiment: Collect circulating copies of 3 benchmarks (mirrors, snapshots), hash-diff them, re-score fixed predictions against variants; pure analysis.

title: Do published improvements stack: the composition test
problem: Each detection paper claims an additive gain over a shared baseline, implying the field's improvements should compose; the composition experiment (apply all of them together) is never run and would test whether claimed gains are real and independent.
hypothesis: Combining the top 8 published compatible improvements from a recent period yields far less than the sum of claimed individual gains, revealing overlap and interference invisible in per-paper evaluations.
cheapest_experiment: Implement the 8 tricks in one codebase, run baseline, individual, and combined configurations with 2 seeds; a bounded grid of training runs.

title: Author-reported vs independently-measured: a systematic reproduction-gap meta-analysis
problem: Reproduction gaps in detection are documented anecdotally; a systematic paired dataset of author-reported vs independently-reproduced numbers would let the field model where gaps come from.
hypothesis: Across 40 reproducible papers, the mean reproduction gap is measurably negative (independent numbers lower), and gap size is predicted by missing reporting fields more than by method complexity.
cheapest_experiment: Aggregate existing third-party reproduction records (model zoos, reproducibility challenges) and fill targeted gaps with 10 new reproductions; mostly data collection.

title: Energy-honest efficiency claims: end-to-end accounting including search
problem: Efficient-detection papers report inference FLOPs while ignoring the search and training energy spent finding the efficient design, so the field cannot say whether efficiency research saves energy at the ecosystem level.
hypothesis: For several published efficient detectors, amortized total energy (search plus training plus deployment) exceeds that of tuning a standard architecture to the same accuracy, unless deployment volume exceeds a computable break-even threshold.
cheapest_experiment: Reconstruct energy budgets from paper disclosures and re-measured training costs, compute break-even curves; measurement plus analysis.

title: Power tables for the field: minimum detectable effects across popular benchmarks
problem: No reference exists telling authors the minimum AP difference each popular benchmark can statistically support, so undersized claims proliferate unchecked by reviewers who lack the numbers.
hypothesis: Publishing bootstrap-derived minimum-detectable-effect tables for 15 popular detection benchmarks shows that a large fraction of recent papers claim differences below their benchmark's resolution threshold.
cheapest_experiment: Bootstrap cached predictions across benchmarks, tabulate minimum detectable effects, cross-reference against claims in 100 papers; re-analysis plus survey.

title: Tuning on the benchmark generalizes worse: the simplicity dividend
problem: Methods heavily tuned on a benchmark may generalize off-benchmark worse than simpler untuned approaches, but this generalization penalty of tuning has not been isolated as a measurable quantity in detection.
hypothesis: Across method pairs matched on COCO AP, the more heavily tuned member (by disclosed search budget) performs systematically worse on a battery of unseen datasets, quantifying a tuning-induced generalization tax.
cheapest_experiment: Select tuned-vs-simple pairs from public checkpoints, evaluate on 8 non-COCO datasets; inference only.

title: Does code release predict smaller reproduction gaps: an observational test
problem: Code release is assumed to guarantee reproducibility, but released code with undocumented configs may reproduce no better than clear papers without code; the actual predictive relationship is unmeasured.
hypothesis: In a matched sample of detection papers, code release alone predicts reproduction-gap size weakly, while config completeness (all hyperparameters and environment pinned) predicts it strongly, redirecting what venues should actually require.
cheapest_experiment: Reproduce 20 papers stratified by code and config completeness, regress gap on disclosure features; bounded reproduction compute.

title: Random configurations as the null hypothesis for architecture components
problem: Published architecture components beat baselines, but the proper null (random configurations from the same design space under the same search budget) is never reported, so component value is confounded with search effort.
hypothesis: Under matched search budgets, random sampling of the design space matches a meaningful fraction of published detection component gains, establishing how much of component research is search rather than insight.
cheapest_experiment: For 2 published design spaces, compare the published component vs best-of-N random configs at the paper's search budget; a bounded grid of short runs.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Coverage-preserving suppression: conformal prediction meets NMS
problem: Conformal prediction can wrap detectors with distribution-free guarantees, but NMS discards the candidate sets those guarantees are computed over, silently destroying coverage; motivation: valid uncertainty must survive the full pipeline, not just the head.
hypothesis: Standard NMS breaks nominal conformal coverage by a measurable margin, and a suppression rule designed to preserve candidate-set coverage restores nominal guarantees at bounded extra prediction-set size.
cheapest_experiment: Measure empirical coverage before and after NMS on cached candidate sets, implement a coverage-aware suppression variant, re-measure; analysis only.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Inpainting as intervention: a causal-evidence benchmark for detection attribution
problem: Attribution methods for detection fail sanity checks partly because evaluation lacks ground-truth causal evidence; motivation: inpainting provides real interventions (remove a region, observe the detection), enabling causal validation of explanations.
hypothesis: An intervention benchmark built from systematic inpainting quantifies attribution methods by causal fidelity, and current methods rank near a trivial box-interior baseline, establishing an honest starting point for detection interpretability.
cheapest_experiment: Generate intervention grids for 300 detections, score 5 attribution methods against measured causal effects; inpainting plus inference.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Machine psychophysics: staircase procedures for measuring detector thresholds
problem: Human vision science measures perceptual thresholds with adaptive staircase procedures giving precise psychometric curves; motivation: detectors deserve the same measurement rigor, replacing coarse benchmark averages with threshold functions (contrast, size, occlusion) per model.
hypothesis: Staircase-measured detection thresholds (minimum contrast, minimum size at fixed reliability) differ across architectures in ways aggregate AP does not predict, and threshold functions predict deployment failures better than AP does.
cheapest_experiment: Implement adaptive staircases over parametric image manipulations for 6 detectors, compare threshold maps vs AP; inference-scale compute.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Item response theory for detection benchmarks: separating instance difficulty from model ability
problem: Benchmark averages conflate model ability with test-item difficulty; motivation: psychometrics solved this with item response theory, which jointly estimates item difficulty and subject ability, enabling adaptive short tests and difficulty-controlled comparisons.
hypothesis: An IRT model fitted on the per-instance outcomes of many detectors compresses benchmark information into ability scores that reproduce full-benchmark rankings using under a tenth of the test set, and flags misfitting items that turn out to be annotation errors.
cheapest_experiment: Fit IRT on the binary per-instance outcome matrix of 30 public detectors on COCO val, validate short-test ranking fidelity and audit misfit items; pure analysis of cached predictions.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Design-based test sets: survey sampling for deployment-valid detection estimates
problem: Test sets are convenience samples, so benchmark estimates carry unknown bias relative to any deployment population; motivation: survey statistics offers design-based sampling and estimators with valid population inference, never applied to detection evaluation.
hypothesis: A stratified probability sample of a deployment image population yields AP estimates with quantified sampling error that differ systematically from convenience-benchmark estimates for the same models, and the direction of the difference is predictable from strata weights.
cheapest_experiment: Define a target population from a public image stream, draw a designed sample, annotate modestly, compare estimates vs convenience benchmarks; annotation-bounded.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Metrology for CV: applying measurement-uncertainty standards to detection evaluation
problem: Engineering metrology has formal standards for stating measurement uncertainty (error budgets, traceability), while CV reports bare point estimates; motivation: importing the error-budget discipline would make benchmark numbers interpretable as measurements.
hypothesis: A full uncertainty budget for COCO AP (annotation noise, sampling error, implementation variance, nondeterminism) shows combined standard uncertainty large enough that many published comparisons are formally inconclusive, and identifies which component to reduce first.
cheapest_experiment: Quantify each budget component from existing sources (re-annotation subsets, bootstrap, cross-framework runs), compose the budget per metrology conventions; mostly analysis.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Optimal experiment design for ablation studies
problem: Ablation grids spend compute uniformly over configurations regardless of information value; motivation: optimal experiment design allocates runs to maximize inferential power per FLOP, which matters as training costs grow.
hypothesis: Sequential design (choosing the next ablation run to maximize expected information about component effects) reaches the same conclusions as exhaustive grids at less than half the compute, validated by replaying published full grids.
cheapest_experiment: Replay 3 published full ablation grids as simulation oracles, compare sequential-design trajectories vs exhaustive ordering; pure simulation on existing numbers.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Extreme value theory for rare detection failures: tail-risk certificates
problem: Safety cases need estimates of worst-case failure frequency, which mean AP cannot provide; motivation: extreme value theory is the statistics of rare events and can extrapolate tail risk from finite evaluation, giving detection a principled safety-estimate methodology.
hypothesis: EVT fitted on per-image failure severities extrapolates the frequency of severe failure events (validated on held-out rare events) within stated confidence, where empirical counting fails for events rarer than the test-set size supports.
cheapest_experiment: Fit EVT models on failure severity distributions from large unlabeled streams scored by an oracle-ish committee, validate extrapolation on held-out data; analysis-scale compute.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Detection as sequential evidence gathering: information-gain evaluation for active perception
problem: Static AP presumes a fixed image, but embodied systems choose viewpoints; motivation: formalizing detection quality as information gain per action connects detection evaluation to the decision problem embodied agents actually solve.
hypothesis: Detectors ranked by static AP reorder substantially when ranked by information gain per view in a controlled multi-view environment, because static AP ignores uncertainty quality that drives view-selection value.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate next-view selection over existing multi-view datasets with several detectors, compare static vs sequential rankings; inference plus simulation.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Actuarial detection: converting AP into expected deployment cost with domain priors
problem: Deployment decisions need expected-cost estimates (missed intrusion, false alarm labor), but detection metrics are cost-blind; motivation: actuarial modeling composes error rates with domain frequency and cost priors into decision-grade numbers.
hypothesis: An actuarial layer over standard detection metrics produces deployment-cost estimates that reverse model choices made on AP alone in realistic scenarios, and the reversal boundary is computable in closed form from cost ratios.
cheapest_experiment: Build cost models for 3 deployment archetypes, evaluate 8 public detectors under them using cached predictions; pure analysis.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Bandit-allocated annotation: regret-minimizing labeling across classes
problem: Annotation budgets are allocated to classes by fixed quotas, ignoring the changing marginal value of labels per class as training progresses; motivation: bandit algorithms are the theory of exactly this allocation-under-uncertainty problem.
hypothesis: A bandit allocator using per-class validation-gain estimates as rewards achieves the same final mAP as quota allocation with substantially fewer labels, with the largest savings in mid-frequency classes.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate label-allocation policies on fully-labeled datasets (labels revealed on demand), compare label-efficiency curves; simulation with short retraining cycles.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Program synthesis of failure slices: automatic discovery of semantic error strata
problem: Error analysis relies on manually chosen slices (size, occlusion), missing unknown semantic failure modes; motivation: program synthesis over interpretable predicates can search the slice space systematically, turning error analysis from art into search.
hypothesis: Synthesized slice programs (compositions of interpretable predicates over metadata and features) recover known failure modes and discover previously unreported ones whose within-slice AP deficit exceeds any manually reported stratum.
cheapest_experiment: Implement predicate search over enriched metadata for cached predictions of 5 detectors, human-validate top discovered slices; analysis-scale compute.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Complementarity-optimal routing between human and detector
problem: Deployed systems route images between models and human reviewers with ad hoc rules; motivation: human-AI complementarity research provides the framework to optimize the joint system rather than the model in isolation, which is what deployment accuracy actually is.
hypothesis: A learned router using model uncertainty and image features achieves joint accuracy above both the best model alone and confidence-threshold routing at matched human workload, with gains concentrated where model confidence is miscalibrated.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate routing on benchmarks using annotator labels as the human channel with measured human error rates, compare routing policies; pure simulation.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Weak-to-strong generalization in dense prediction: when can weak teachers train stronger students
problem: Auto-labeling assumes teacher quality upper-bounds student quality, but weak-to-strong results in language models suggest otherwise; motivation: establishing whether and when students exceed their detection teachers determines the economics of every pseudo-labeling pipeline.
hypothesis: Students with stronger backbones trained purely on weak-teacher detection labels exceed teacher AP under identifiable conditions (teacher errors uncorrelated with image features the student can access), and fail to when teacher errors are systematic.
cheapest_experiment: Train strong students on labels from deliberately weakened teachers with controlled error structure; a grid of short training runs.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Shard Shapley: data valuation for detection at practical granularity
problem: Data purchasing and pruning decisions need value estimates per data source, but Shapley-style valuation is intractable per image; motivation: valuing shards (sources, batches) instead of images makes principled data valuation computationally feasible for detection.
hypothesis: Shard-level Shapley values computed via truncated sampling identify low-value or harmful data sources whose removal improves AP per training FLOP, and the values transfer across model scales within a family.
cheapest_experiment: Partition training data into 20 shards, estimate Shapley values with truncated Monte Carlo over short trainings, validate by removal; many short runs at small scale.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Behavioral contracts for detector updates: regression testing beyond AP
problem: Model updates that preserve AP can still silently change which instances are detected, breaking downstream systems; motivation: software engineering's contract testing formalizes behavioral compatibility, which detection deployment currently lacks entirely.
hypothesis: AP-matched checkpoint updates flip detection outcomes on a substantial fraction of instances (behavioral churn), and a contract suite (protected-instance sets with flip budgets) can be satisfied with negligible AP cost, making low-churn updates practical.
cheapest_experiment: Measure churn across public checkpoint successions, then finetune with a churn penalty on protected sets; analysis plus one training run.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Cohort studies on deployment logs: observational epidemiology of detector failure
problem: Deployment logs record failures under uncontrolled conditions, and naive failure statistics are confounded; motivation: epidemiology's cohort and case-control designs extract causal risk factors from exactly this kind of observational data.
hypothesis: Case-control analysis of deployment-style logs (matched failure and success cohorts) identifies risk factors for detection failure (lighting, density, motion) with effect sizes that replicate in controlled re-tests, validating observational methodology for model monitoring.
cheapest_experiment: Construct cohorts from public video-stream benchmarks with known failures, run matched analyses, verify top factors in controlled evaluation; analysis-scale.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Queueing-aware detection: accuracy under frame-drop policies as a co-design problem
problem: Video analytics systems drop frames under load, and the interaction between drop policies and detection temporal characteristics determines system accuracy; motivation: queueing theory models the load process, enabling principled co-design instead of independent tuning.
hypothesis: Under realistic arrival processes, detection-aware drop policies (drop frames the detector handles worst or redundantly) beat FIFO dropping by a margin that grows with load, computable from queueing parameters plus per-frame detection value curves.
cheapest_experiment: Simulate load traces over video benchmarks with several drop policies and 3 detectors; pure simulation.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Uncertainty cartography: decision-quality evaluation of detection-map visualization
problem: Aerial and geospatial detection outputs feed human decisions through maps, and GIS has a mature uncertainty-visualization literature that CV ignores; motivation: the scientific question is whether communicating detection uncertainty spatially changes decision quality, which is measurable.
hypothesis: Decision-makers using uncertainty-annotated detection maps make measurably better resource-allocation decisions (in a controlled task) than those using standard confidence-thresholded maps, with the gain concentrated in low-density ambiguous regions.
cheapest_experiment: Controlled user study (30 participants) on a simulated allocation task over real aerial detection outputs with and without uncertainty encoding; small study.

cluster: New combinations with genuine scientific motivation
title: Likelihood ratios for detection evidence: forensic reporting standards for CV
problem: Courts and audits consume detection outputs as evidence, but scores are not calibrated evidence statements; motivation: forensic statistics developed likelihood-ratio frameworks precisely to convert measurements into legally interpretable evidence strength.
hypothesis: A likelihood-ratio wrapper over detector scores (calibrated against defined hypothesis pairs) produces evidence statements that are empirically well-calibrated across conditions where raw scores mislead by orders of magnitude, establishing feasibility of forensic-grade detection reporting.
cheapest_experiment: Fit and validate LR calibration on benchmark data under shifted conditions for one deployment-style scenario; analysis only.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Half the remaining COCO errors are not model errors
problem: The narrative that detection still has headroom on COCO assumes residual errors reflect model deficiency; if most are annotation artifacts, the field is optimizing against noise and needs new benchmarks more than new methods.
hypothesis: Human adjudication shows that at least half of a SOTA detector's residual COCO errors (misses and false positives at deployment thresholds) are attributable to ground-truth problems rather than model failure.
cheapest_experiment: Adjudicate 1,000 stratified residual errors of one SOTA model with 2 independent annotators and a tie-breaker; small annotation budget, no training.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: 2015 architecture, 2026 recipe: how much progress is training practice
problem: A decade of detection progress mixes architectural innovation with recipe improvements (augmentation, schedules, pretraining), and the field has never decomposed the total gain into these two components.
hypothesis: Faster R-CNN with a modern backbone-agnostic recipe (current augmentation, schedule, and pretrained initialization of its original backbone family) closes most of the gap to modern architectures on COCO, attributing the bulk of decade-scale progress to recipes rather than architecture.
cheapest_experiment: Train the legacy architecture under a curated modern recipe and compare against matched modern models; a few training runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: A 1k-image subset ranks detectors as well as the full benchmark
problem: Evaluation on full benchmarks is assumed necessary for reliable rankings, inflating iteration costs across the field; the actual subset size sufficient for stable rankings is unmeasured.
hypothesis: A difficulty-stratified 1,000-image COCO subset reproduces full-val detector rankings with rank correlation above 0.95 across 30 public models, making most full-set evaluations during development wasteful.
cheapest_experiment: Optimize and validate subset selection against cached full-val results of 30 checkpoints; pure re-analysis.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Learned proposals contribute nothing at modern scale
problem: Two-stage detectors learn region proposals on the premise that learned localization priors matter; with modern backbones the proposal stage may be replaceable by fixed geometric priors without loss, changing how the two-stage story is told.
hypothesis: Replacing the learned proposal network with a fixed dense grid of geometric priors (matched count) costs under half an AP point on COCO with a modern backbone, showing the learned stage has become vestigial.
cheapest_experiment: Two matched training runs (learned proposals vs fixed priors) on one two-stage detector with a modern backbone; two training runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Augmentation is just data: gains recoverable by more images
problem: Augmentation is treated as qualitatively special, but its gains may be entirely substitutable by additional real data, which would reframe augmentation research as a data-economics question.
hypothesis: For each standard augmentation policy there exists a data-volume increment that reproduces its AP gain exactly, and the exchange rate (augmentation value in image-equivalents) is stable across scales, making augmentation and data fungible.
cheapest_experiment: Train a grid over augmentation on-off and data fractions, fit the exchange-rate curve; a bounded grid of short runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Localization is solved; classification is the bottleneck
problem: Detection research allocates enormous effort to localization machinery, but error decompositions may show classification confusion dominates remaining error, misaligning research investment with the actual bottleneck.
hypothesis: For modern detectors on COCO, replacing predicted boxes with GT boxes (oracle localization) improves AP far less than replacing predicted labels with GT labels (oracle classification), across architectures.
cheapest_experiment: Run both oracle substitutions on cached predictions of 6 detectors; pure re-analysis.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Detectors barely use global context: the cropping test
problem: Architectures increasingly pursue global context aggregation on the assumption detection needs it, but the measurable contribution of context beyond a local window around each object is surprisingly undocumented.
hypothesis: Evaluating detectors on tight local crops around GT neighborhoods (context removed beyond 2x object size) preserves the large majority of full-image AP, bounding the value of global context far below what architecture trends assume.
cheapest_experiment: Crop-based evaluation protocol on COCO val for 5 detectors; inference only.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Silhouettes are almost enough: shape suffices for most detection classes
problem: The texture-bias literature implies detectors need texture, but for detection (unlike classification) object shape and layout may carry most class evidence, which would change robustness strategy fundamentally.
hypothesis: Detectors evaluated on silhouette-rendered scenes (shapes filled with flat color, layout preserved) retain the majority of AP for most COCO categories, contradicting the texture-primacy narrative for detection.
cheapest_experiment: Render silhouette versions of COCO val using GT masks, evaluate 5 detectors; rendering plus inference.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: NMS-free wins are tuning artifacts
problem: End-to-end NMS-free detectors are claimed to beat NMS pipelines, but the NMS baselines are rarely given equivalent post-processing tuning effort, leaving the core claim uncontrolled.
hypothesis: After matched tuning of classical NMS variants (thresholds, soft-NMS, class-wise settings), the reported advantage of NMS-free architectures on standard benchmarks disappears within seed noise.
cheapest_experiment: Exhaustive post-processing tuning for matched NMS-based checkpoints against published NMS-free results; inference-scale tuning.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Label assignment research stops mattering at scale
problem: A large literature optimizes label assignment (which predictions get supervised), validated at modest scale; if assignment differences wash out with strong pretraining and data scale, the subfield's relevance window has closed.
hypothesis: With foundation-scale pretraining and modern data volume, assignment strategies that differed by multiple AP points at 2020 scale differ by less than seed noise, demonstrating scale subsumption of assignment research.
cheapest_experiment: Train 3 assignment strategies at two scale points (2020-style vs modern pretrained); six training runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Epoch-1 validation predicts final ranking
problem: Model development assumes full training is needed to compare configurations, making search expensive; if very-early validation AP already predicts final ordering, most search compute is wasted.
hypothesis: Across a diverse configuration pool, validation AP after one epoch rank-correlates above 0.9 with final AP, enabling early stopping of experimental comparisons at a tenth of current cost.
cheapest_experiment: Log early and final AP over a pool of 30 short-to-full training configurations at small scale; a pool of short runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Random boxes teach detection: how little box supervision quality matters early
problem: Weakly-supervised detection invests in mining good boxes from classification data, but early training may only need any plausible spatial prior, with box quality mattering only late, which would invert pipeline design.
hypothesis: Pretraining detection heads with random-but-plausible boxes on classification data, then briefly finetuning with real boxes, matches full box-supervised training curves after a small fraction of labeled-box exposure.
cheapest_experiment: Compare random-box pretraining plus short finetune vs full supervision at matched budgets; a few short training runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: The small-object ceiling is human, not machine
problem: Small-object detection is framed as a model limitation, but humans may disagree with GT as much as SOTA models do on small objects, meaning the reported gap to perfection is an annotation mirage below some size.
hypothesis: Below a measurable size threshold, human annotators re-labeling benchmark images agree with original GT no better than SOTA detectors do, locating the size floor beneath which benchmark-driven progress claims are unfalsifiable.
cheapest_experiment: Human re-annotation of size-stratified samples, compare human-GT vs model-GT agreement curves by size; small annotation budget.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Only rank matters: confidence magnitudes carry no deployable information
problem: Calibration research assumes score magnitudes matter beyond ranking, but every standard detection consumer (NMS, AP, top-k) is rank-invariant, so magnitude information may be operationally worthless in current pipelines.
hypothesis: Replacing detector confidences with rank-preserving arbitrary magnitudes changes no standard pipeline output (AP, NMS results, threshold-swept F1 curves up to reparameterization), while breaking exactly the downstream uses (fusion, routing) that justify calibration research, cleanly separating where magnitudes matter.
cheapest_experiment: Apply rank-preserving score transformations across pipelines and downstream fusion tasks, catalog invariances; pure analysis.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Resolution is nothing but object pixel count
problem: Input resolution is treated as a global quality knob, but its entire effect on detection may reduce to the pixel count on each object, which would collapse resolution research into a single per-object variable.
hypothesis: At matched object-pixel counts (achieved by cropping vs scaling), detection accuracy per instance is statistically indistinguishable across input resolutions, proving object pixels, not image resolution, is the causal variable.
cheapest_experiment: Construct matched object-pixel evaluations via crop-scale manipulations of the same instances, evaluate 4 detectors; inference only.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Batched inference cross-talk: your detections depend on your batchmates
problem: Deployments batch images through adaptive components (batch-statistics layers, TTA-style adaptive normalization), so one image's detections may depend on unrelated batchmates, violating the independence users assume; the effect size is unmeasured.
hypothesis: For deployment configurations using any batch-adaptive statistics, per-image detection outputs change measurably with batch composition, and the effect is exploitable (a crafted batchmate suppresses another image's detections).
cheapest_experiment: Permute batch compositions at inference across adaptive configurations of 3 detectors, measure output deltas and craft one adversarial batchmate; inference-scale compute.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Scale beats diversity at fixed budget: testing the diversity dogma for detection data
problem: Data-collection wisdom says diverse sources beat volume, but at fixed labeling budget the trade has never been cleanly measured for detection, leaving collection strategy to intuition.
hypothesis: At matched labeled-image budgets, single-domain volume matches multi-domain diversity for in-domain deployment AP and loses only under explicit domain shift, quantifying exactly when diversity is worth its coordination cost.
cheapest_experiment: Compose matched training budgets at 4 diversity levels from existing multi-domain datasets, train matched detectors, test in- and out-of-domain; a grid of short runs.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Coarse features already solve fine-grained detection classification
problem: Fine-grained detection is assumed to require specialized feature learning, but frozen coarse features plus a linear readout may already contain the needed distinctions, which would redirect fine-grained research toward data rather than features.
hypothesis: Linear probes on frozen general-detector instance features match end-to-end fine-grained detection heads on subcategory classification given matched labels, showing the bottleneck is supervision, not representation.
cheapest_experiment: Probe frozen instance features vs finetuned heads on a fine-grained detection dataset; probe training only.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Instructions beat annotators: labeling-protocol effects exceed inter-annotator noise
problem: Dataset quality discussions focus on annotator skill and count, but the instruction document may be the dominant factor, with protocol wording changing what a dataset even measures; this is testable and never tested for detection.
hypothesis: The same images annotated under two reasonable instruction variants (differing in box-tightness and ambiguity rules) produce GT differing enough that a fixed model's AP changes by more than the inter-annotator variance within either protocol.
cheapest_experiment: A-B instruction experiment on 300 images with 3 annotators per arm, evaluate fixed models against both GTs; small annotation budget.

cluster: Simple hypotheses that challenge accepted beliefs
title: Foundation-model detection advantage partly reduces to test-set exposure
problem: Foundation-model detectors beat traditional baselines on public benchmarks, but their pretraining crawls may contain benchmark test images or near-duplicates, and the exposure-attributable share of their advantage is unmeasured.
hypothesis: On verified-clean test splits (no near-duplicates in pretraining crawls), the advantage of web-pretrained detection models over dataset-pretrained baselines shrinks measurably relative to standard test splits, attributing part of the foundation-model advantage to exposure.
cheapest_experiment: Partition existing test sets by pretraining-crawl duplicate detection where crawl indices are public, compare model gaps on clean vs exposed partitions; analysis plus inference.
